title: consent/approve-request/0.1: an unsigned document rendered on a human's phone, invisible to every census
body:
## Summary

`vta-service` constructs a `consent/approve-request/0.1` Trust Task document and buffers it to an approver's mediator for delivery to their phone, where a human is asked to approve something. It carries **no `proof`**, and **no census in this repo can see it**.

## Verified facts

**No proof.** `vta-service/src/trust_tasks/consent.rs:411` builds the document inline:

```rust
let approve_request = serde_json::json!({
    "id": format!("urn:uuid:{}", Uuid::new_v4()),
    "type": CONSENT_APPROVE_REQUEST_TYPE,
    "issuedAt": chrono::Utc::now().to_rfc3339_opts(chrono::SecondsFormat::Secs, true),
    "payload": prompt_payload,
});
```

`id`, `type`, `issuedAt`, `payload`. That is the whole document.

**The comparable path does gate on a proof.** `vta-mobile-core/src/task.rs:93`, parsing `auth/step-up/approve-request`:

```rust
// The gate: no valid proof from an enrolled executor, no prompt.
let relying_party = crate::proof::verify_signed_request(&v, &trusted_issuers).await?;
```

The consent prompt has no equivalent parser and no proof. Both end up in front of a person being asked to authorise something.

**No spec.** `https://trusttasks.org/spec/consent/approve-request/0.1` is not in the registry. `consent/request/1.0` is the requester-side task, not the approver prompt, and `auth/step-up/approve-request/0.2` is a different ceremony — neither is a fold target.

## Why nothing catches it

Three harnesses exist and each misses it for a different reason:

1. **`UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS`** (`vta-service/src/trust_tasks/mod.rs:237`) is shrink-only and fails the build on a new unspecced URI — but it tracks URIs this service **serves**. This one is only ever **produced**.
2. **`producer_payload_conformance.rs`** covers client methods in `vta-sdk` that build payloads by hand. This document is constructed inline in `vta-service`, through no client method.
3. **`trust_task_manifest.rs`**'s census (`BINDING_SITES`) does not scan `vta-service/src` — but note that adding it **would not help**, and an earlier read of this suggested it would. That census's `PREFIX` is `https://trusttasks.org/openvtc/vtc/` (`trust_task_manifest.rs:25`), the VTC's private namespace. This URI is in the public `spec/` namespace, so the scan would not match it wherever it ran.

So the gap is structural: **there is no census over outbound producer URIs in the public namespace.** Serving one is caught; producing one is not.

## Why it matters

The named risk is not schema drift. It is that the one thing standing between an attacker and a human tapping "approve" is whatever the mediator and transport authenticate — with nothing in the document itself for the device to verify against an enrolled issuer, which is precisely the check the step-up path performs.

## Suggested fix

1. Give the document a `proof`, signed with the VTA's issuer key — the same key task-consent requests and step-up approve-requests are signed with (`operations::credentials::load_vta_issuer_secret`).
2. Verify it device-side before rendering a prompt, mirroring `parse_step_up_request`.
3. Publish `consent/approve-request/0.1` with `proof` REQUIRED, so the requirement is normative rather than local.
4. Close the structural hole: extend the tracked-debt harness to cover **produced** URIs, not just served ones, so the next inline-constructed document is visible the day it lands.

## Not a release blocker

This ships today and is not a regression introduced by the pending release. Filing it so it is tracked rather than rediscovered from a rejected request in production — which is how the two shipped payload defects (#895, #919) were found.

title: release(core): @openvtc/pnm-core 0.5.0
body:
npm has served 0.4.0 since 2026-08-17, which predates everything from #123
onward. Diffing the published tarball's runtime exports against this build: 35
added, one removed (`markInboundHandled`). `matchesTrustTaskCode` does not
appear as removed because it never shipped — it landed in #126, after 0.4.0 was
cut — so deleting it broke nothing for a consumer.

Breaking under 0.x rules, hence the leading component: the inbound de-dup call
changed shape, the vault and passkey wire types became the generated ones (a
non-empty `targets`, an optional `transports`, an attachment digest that is
`digestMultibase` rather than hex), and `@cfworker/json-schema` is a new runtime
dependency. The changelog leads with a Migration section for exactly those.

Also refreshes the two runtime dependencies this package actually ships —
`@noble/curves` ^2.4.0, `cbor-x` ^1.6.6, both in-range, no advisories. The
toolchain and UI dependencies of the private workspaces are left alone; `vite`
in particular touches the MV3 bundle and should be attributable to its own
commit.

Corrects one stale claim in the changelog while here: the `admin` entry said the
agent implements `internal` on `keys/create` and `origin: "internal"` with the
published schema having neither. The schema has both now, and the local
widenings were removed in #127.

`packages/extension` and `packages/pwa` move to `^0.5.0`; their old `^0.4.0`
would not have resolved to it.

title: fix(inbound): enforce the published schema on a consent payload (#128)
body:
fix(inbound): enforce the published schema on a consent payload (#128)

* fix(inbound): enforce the published schema on a consent payload

A `sideEffects` value the schema forbids rendered to the human as the *safest*
thing the consent surface can draw.

`parseTaskConsentRequest` checked the payload with a hand-written block of
`typeof` tests. Those are not a cheap version of the schema — they ask weaker
questions, and in one place the difference reached a human.
`typeof payload.sideEffects !== "string"` admits any string; the schema admits
`none`, `mutating` or `destructive`. `confirm.tsx` renders severity by
comparing against those three:

    background: destructive ? danger : sideEffects === "mutating" ? warn : ok

so anything outside the enum — a typo, a re-cased value, a value from a peer
that disagrees about the contract — fell through to the `ok` branch and was
painted green, with the unrecognised string as its label. The most dangerous
outcome a schema violation can produce was presented as the most reassuring.

The same gap ran through the rest of the payload: `minApprovals` was checked as
a `number` where the schema says integer >= 1, so `0` passed and a surface would
have shown a threshold nothing has to meet; `effects` was `Array.isArray` with
no element shape; `exposure` was any object at all; `note` — bounded to 500 by
framework 0.5 §7.3 item 19 *precisely* so a consent surface is not handed
unbounded prose — was not checked; and `additionalProperties: false` went
unenforced, so a member the schema forbids arrived silently.

Validating the published schema also found a live drift it was not looking for:
the fixtures for this family still carried the *hex* form of the shared
cross-repo digest, long after the multibase cutover. `typeof === "string"` had
accepted it every time; the schema's `DigestMultibase` pattern did not.

**Why a real validator rather than a subset of one.** Surveying the 349 payload
schemas this package ships finds `$ref` 2583 times, `oneOf` 141,
`propertyNames` 669, `pattern` 1036, `format` 944, plus `not`, `uniqueItems`,
`dependentRequired` and `minProperties`. A partial implementation of that
under-enforces silently, which is worse than not validating — it reports success
it did not establish. `@cfworker/json-schema` is a complete 2020-12
implementation with no dependencies of its own, and this is the keyword set that
makes `unevaluatedProperties` enforceable at all: no generated *type*, in either
language, can express it (trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#327 fixes the Rust
side of that, and has no TypeScript counterpart to fix because TS types are
structural and never rejected an unknown member at runtime).

`@openvtc/trust-tasks` deliberately ships no validator — zero runtime deps so it
loads anywhere — and defines the consumer seam instead. `trust-tasks/validate.ts`
fills it, compiles each schema once against a `WeakMap` keyed by the schema
object (the inbound path revalidates on every mediator redelivery after a worker
respawn), and reports every violation rather than the first. `validatePayload`
on `ParseTaskConsentOptions` lets a caller substitute a different validator;
there is deliberately no way to switch validation off, and an unusable schema
refuses rather than passes.

Cost: `offscreen` 167 -> 206 kB (45 -> 58 kB gzipped). `background.js` is
unchanged at 48 kB — the consent path is not in the service worker, so the MV3
single-bundle invariant is untouched.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(deps): take trust-tasks 0.16.2, which makes provision/integration/0.3 satisfiable

0.16.0 shipped that spec's `$defs/Response` requiring `digest` while its
`properties` carried only `digestMultibase` — the member the 0.2 -> 0.3 rename
replaced. The object is closed, so the schema admits nothing: a consumer that
validated a conforming response would have rejected it.

Upstream #324 corrected the schema and regenerated the Rust bindings but not the
TypeScript ones, so the two libraries disagreed about the wire contract until
#326 ran `build-ts-bindings` as well. That is the failure `check-bindings`
exists to catch, and did.

It mattered here only because this branch starts executing the schemas this
package ships rather than merely carrying them. So it comes with a guard: a
sweep asserting no shipped schema has a `required` naming a member its
`properties` does not define, where the object is closed — the cheap, decidable
half of satisfiability, and the half that would have caught this. All 349
schemas pass on 0.16.2.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: feat(core): adopt Trust Tasks 0.16.0, and close the specced-family gap (#127)
body:
feat(core): adopt Trust Tasks 0.16.0, and close the specced-family gap (#127)

Brings the repo onto `@openvtc/trust-tasks` 0.16.0 — which is the content the
Rust side calls 0.17.0; the two packages version their own APIs, not `SPEC.md`,
so there is no TypeScript 0.17 to wait for.

The bump itself needed no source change. What it surfaced did.

**SPEC §7.2 item 11 was not implemented.** `inbound/dedup.ts` recorded bare ids
and answered "seen / not seen", which cannot express the half of item 11 that
matters: a *different* document under a used `id` MUST be refused as
`idConflict`, not absorbed. It also keyed on the DIDComm message id — the
transport identifier §7.2 names explicitly as one that MUST NOT substitute for
the document `id`, and the one a mediator is free to change on redelivery.
`claimInboundDocument` now returns fresh/duplicate/conflict, keyed on the
document's own id plus a digest of its RFC 8785 canonicalization, so a
re-serializing intermediary cannot turn a §8.4 retry into a conflict. Durable
via KVStore, because MV3 tears the worker down mid-decision.

`idConflict` was also landing in `e.p.msg.bad_request` on the send path: it
postdates `coerceTrustTaskCode`'s switch, and is why the framework runtimes emit
`trust-task-error/0.5` — 0.3's enum cannot carry it. The standard/extended split
now comes from the runtime's `normalizeCode`/`isStandardCode` rather than a
local regex that also rewrote extended codes containing `_`.

**Coverage 130 -> 152 of 177.** Every family that is specced, published as a
binding, and named by `vta-sdk` is now implemented: `trust-task-discovery/0.1`,
`acl/update`, `vta/webvh/servers/retire-orphan`, `vtc/members/removal-notice`
(a parser — the wallet receives it), `vta/app-state/*` (6, new module),
`vta/services/*` (8), `vta/credentials/{issue,revoke}`, and
`auth/passkey/login/{start,finish}/0.2`. All 25 outstanding are unspecced, so
the number now moves when upstream lands a spec rather than when someone here
finds time.

**Versions.** `vtc/join-requests/submit` 0.1 -> 0.2 (a four-outcome `verdict`
replaces `status: "pending"`, so applicants who had been *admitted* were being
reported as pending); `vault/{list,get,upsert}` and `provision/integration` to
0.3 and `device/wipe` to 0.2 once VTI landed them; `vta/credentials/issue` to
0.2, which VTI shipped as a removal rather than a deprecation. No bare-hex wire
digest remains.

**Hand-copied wire types replaced by the generated ones** in `vta/protocol.ts`,
`vault/list.ts` and `provision/send.ts`. Each copy had drifted: `transports` was
typed required when the schema says optional (and used a DOM type in the
transport-free layer), the vault entry was written from `_shared/0.1` while the
module posted 0.2 and had lost the non-empty `targets` constraint, and
`keys/create` was missing `keyId` — the field `vta-sdk` 0.30.0 was cut for, and
not optional in practice for an `internal` key, which has no derivation path to
be named after.

**Compatibility folds removed.** Nothing is deployed — no Web Store release, no
consumers — so the trust-tasks #279 dual-accept and a legacy inbound-dedup
record were dead code that read like live constraints. VTI emits only the
current spelling; verified before deleting. Recorded as a rule in CLAUDE.md so
it is not reintroduced.

CI's admin-isolation check now names the two new `admin/` modules, and the
task-surface snapshot is refreshed to vta-sdk 0.30.0.

title: trust-tasks-rs-v0.17.2
body:
### Fixed

- **codegen**: Carry unevaluatedProperties strictness into the generated type ([#327](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/327))

* fix(codegen): carry unevaluatedProperties strictness into the generated type

  A specification that reuses a shared definition and adds members of its own
  has exactly one way to close the result: `unevaluatedProperties` at the
  outer level. `additionalProperties` cannot do it — both keywords are
  evaluated against the whole instance from within the subschema that declares
  them, so one inside either the shared definition or the composing schema
  rejects the other's members. That is why `credentials/_shared/0.2`'s
  `IssuedCredentialBase` is deliberately left open and
  `vta/credentials/issue/0.2` closes over it.

  typify does not model `unevaluatedProperties`. It flattens the `allOf` into
  a single struct carrying every member — the right shape — but emits no
  `deny_unknown_fields`, because it maps only `additionalProperties: false`.
  The generated type is then more permissive than the schema it came from: a
  validator rejects an unknown member, the Rust type silently accepts it.

  `issue/0.1` closes with `additionalProperties` and generates
  `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]`. `issue/0.2` says the same thing the only
  way a composition can, and generated nothing. That is a silent weakening
  across a version bump whose whole purpose was to stop the two definitions
  drifting.

  This flattens the composition before typify sees it, so the strictness
  survives. The struct is unchanged; only the attribute is added.

  Two things it deliberately does not do:

  - It runs after `raw` is captured, so `PAYLOAD_SCHEMA` still carries the
    published `allOf` + `unevaluatedProperties` text. Runtime validation is
    against the real schema, not this rewrite.
  - It declines any composition whose members are not plain object schemas —
    a nested combinator, an `if`/`then`, a member that closes itself, an
    unresolvable `$ref`. The merge would not be sound there, and a wrong
    `deny_unknown_fields` rejects valid documents, which is worse than the
    permissiveness it would fix.

  Only `vta/credentials/issue/0.2` uses the pattern today, so the regenerated
  output is one file. It is the composition style the registry is moving
  toward, which is why it is worth fixing at the generator.

title: chore(deps): azure_identity 1.0, with the Key Vault bump it requires
body:
Replaces Dependabot's #1169, which bumped `azure_identity` alone and failed with:

```
error[E0277]: the trait bound `DeveloperToolsCredential:
             azure_core::credentials::TokenCredential` is not satisfied
note: there are multiple different versions of crate `azure_core` in the dependency graph
```

That second line is the whole story, and it's easy to read past. **Nothing about `DeveloperToolsCredential` changed.**

| crate | azure_core |
|---|---|
| `azure_identity` 1.0 | 1.1 |
| `azure_security_keyvault_secrets` 0.14 | 0.35 |

The credential implements 1.1's `TokenCredential`; `SecretClient::new` wants 0.35's. Same trait by name, a different trait to the compiler.

This is the **same shape as #1166** (k8s-openapi / kube): Dependabot bumped one half of a coupled pair, and the resulting error names a type rather than the version skew that produced it. So `azure_security_keyvault_secrets` goes 0.14 → 1.0 alongside, and the lockfile is back to exactly one `azure_core`.

**No source changes.** `SecretClient::new(vault_url, credential, None)` and the `DeveloperToolsCredential::new` call are identical across both majors.

- `cargo check --workspace --all-features` clean
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets` → 0
- `cargo test -p vti-secrets --features azure-secrets` passes

Closes #1169.

title: chore(deps): k8s-openapi 0.28, with the kube bump it requires
body:
Replaces Dependabot's #1166, which bumped `k8s-openapi` alone and failed with:

```
None of the v1_* features are enabled on the k8s-openapi crate.
```

…pointing at **`k8s-openapi v0.27.1`** — a version the PR had just moved away from. The message names the copy that has no version feature rather than the mismatch that produced it, which is what makes it read as a feature-declaration problem when it's a resolution one.

`kube` depends on a specific `k8s-openapi` major:

| kube | k8s-openapi |
|---|---|
| 3.1 | 0.27 |
| 4.2 | 0.28 |

Bumping only `k8s-openapi` puts **two copies** in the tree, and the workspace's `features = ["latest"]` applies to just one. The other has none, and its build script panics. k8s-openapi's own error text says exactly this — *"check your Cargo.lock or run `cargo tree -i k8s-openapi` to ensure that this version is the only one being used"* — but it's easy to read past when the error names a version you thought you'd removed.

So the two move together. `kube` 3.1 → 4.2 leaves exactly one `k8s-openapi` in the lockfile, and the comment above the declaration now records why they're coupled, so the next bump doesn't rediscover it.

**No source changes.** The core/v1 `Secret` shape this backend uses is long-stable and `Client::try_default()` is unchanged across the major.

- `cargo check --workspace --all-features` clean
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets` → 0
- `cargo test -p vti-secrets --features k8s-secrets` passes

Closes #1166.

| | closes with | generated |
|---|---|---|
| `issue/0.1` | `additionalProperties: false` | `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` |
| `issue/0.2` | `unevaluatedProperties: false` | *(nothing)* |

So the generated type is **more permissive than the schema it came from**: a validator rejects an unknown member, the Rust type silently accepts it. That's a silent weakening across a version bump whose whole purpose was to stop two definitions drifting.

Found by the VTI conformance sweep, whose drifted-witness check asserts the generated type rejects an unknown member. It failed on 0.2 and passed on 0.1.

### The fix

Flatten the composition before typify sees it, so the strictness survives the round-trip. The struct typify produces is unchanged; only the attribute is added.

Two things it deliberately does **not** do:

- **It runs after `raw` is captured**, so `PAYLOAD_SCHEMA` still carries the published `allOf` + `unevaluatedProperties` text. Runtime validation is against the real published schema, not this rewrite. Verified on the regenerated output.
- **It declines** any composition whose members aren't plain object schemas — a nested combinator, an `if`/`then`, a member that closes itself, an unresolvable `$ref`. The merge wouldn't be sound there, and a wrong `deny_unknown_fields` rejects valid documents, which is worse than the permissiveness it fixes. Each decline path has a test.

### Regenerated output

One file: `trust-tasks-rs/src/specs/vta/credentials/issue/v0_2.rs`, gaining `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` on `Response`. Only `issue/0.2` uses the pattern today, but it's the composition style the registry is moving toward, which is why it's worth fixing at the generator rather than per-spec.

`cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --all-features` and `cargo test -p trust-tasks-codegen` green; workspace clippy 0.

title: fix(codegen): carry unevaluatedProperties strictness into the generated type (#327)

fix(codegen): carry unevaluatedProperties strictness into the generated type (#327)

* fix(codegen): carry unevaluatedProperties strictness into the generated type

A specification that reuses a shared definition and adds members of its own
has exactly one way to close the result: `unevaluatedProperties` at the
outer level. `additionalProperties` cannot do it — both keywords are
evaluated against the whole instance from within the subschema that declares
them, so one inside either the shared definition or the composing schema
rejects the other's members. That is why `credentials/_shared/0.2`'s
`IssuedCredentialBase` is deliberately left open and
`vta/credentials/issue/0.2` closes over it.

typify does not model `unevaluatedProperties`. It flattens the `allOf` into
a single struct carrying every member — the right shape — but emits no
`deny_unknown_fields`, because it maps only `additionalProperties: false`.
The generated type is then more permissive than the schema it came from: a
validator rejects an unknown member, the Rust type silently accepts it.

way a composition can, and generated nothing. That is a silent weakening
across a version bump whose whole purpose was to stop the two definitions
drifting.

survives. The struct is unchanged; only the attribute is added.

  unresolvable `$ref`. The merge would not be sound there, and a wrong
  `deny_unknown_fields` rejects valid documents, which is worse than the

title: chore(deps)!: aes-gcm 0.11, and stop the nonce conversions panicking
body:
Replaces Dependabot's #1167, which was red on **ten** checks. 0.11 removes two things this workspace was reaching through the cipher rather than depending on directly.

### `aead::OsRng` is gone

Nine sites across five crates generated nonces and salts through `aes_gcm::aead::OsRng` — a re-export, borrowing whatever CSPRNG the cipher happened to vendor. They now use `rand::rng()`, which is what the rest of the workspace already uses for exactly this. `vta-backup` gains a direct `rand` dependency it always needed and was getting by accident.

### `aead::generic_array` became `hybrid_array`

The `GenericArray::from_slice` calls in `vta-tee`'s KMS bootstrap move to the public `Key` / `Nonce` aliases — infallible `.into()` where the source is a fixed-size array, `try_from` where it's a runtime slice out of a CMS envelope.

### The part worth reading

Not required by the bump. `Nonce::from_slice` is deprecated in favour of `TryFrom`, and CI runs clippy with `-D warnings`, so all nineteen call sites had to move. **They were not equivalent.**

`from_slice` **panics** on a wrong length, and every one of those sites parses a stored or transmitted blob. `vta-backup` already knew:

```rust
// Hard length check before `Nonce::from_slice` — the `aes-gcm` impl of that
// constructor panics on the wrong length, which a crafted backup envelope
// would otherwise weaponise into a process-killing DoS on `/backup/import`.
```

…with regression tests for it. That hand-written guard was the only thing between the parser and the panic, and it had to be remembered at every new call site.

With `TryFrom` the panic is gone **by construction**. The length checks stay, because they produce the better error — `invalid nonce length: 11 (expected 12)` rather than a bare conversion failure — but they're no longer load-bearing for safety, and the comments now say so. The DoS regression tests stay too: they assert the *rejection*, which is still the contract.

One site was genuinely reachable rather than defence-in-depth: `vta-keys::wrapping` unwrapping a wire-supplied nonce, where the length is attacker-controlled and nothing checked it first.

### Verification

- clippy **0** across the workspace, all features, all targets
- the crypto crates' **146 tests** pass — including the CMS envelope round-trip and the wrong-length-nonce DoS regressions
- `vtc-service` 866 pass; full `cargo test --workspace --all-features` clean

Closes #1167.

title: fix(ci): stop Dependabot emitting chore(deps)(deps) titles, and let a fixed title clear the check
body:
Every cargo PR Dependabot opened in its first hour is red on `commit lint`:

```
#1170 chore(deps)(deps): bump tower-http from 0.6.11 to 0.7.0
#1169 chore(deps)(deps): bump azure_identity from 0.35.0 to 1.0.0
...
```

`include: scope` appends the scope itself, so a `prefix` that already carries one doubles it. The commit-lint job checks the **PR title** against the conventional-commit regex, which rejects `chore(deps)(deps):` — a check failing for a reason unrelated to the bump, on every PR, which is the fastest way to teach people to ignore it.

My bug, from #1160 an hour ago. The `github-actions` and `docker` entries were already correct — they set a scoped prefix and *don't* set `include`, which is the other consistent way to spell it. I'll retitle the six open ones by hand, since the check reads the title rather than the branch's commit messages.

title: Specify both VMC directions so membership requires member consent
body:
The spec asserted in five places that two VMCs form a complete membership edge, but the normative schema required `issuer` to be the VTC/VTN C-DID and the subject to be the member, making the reverse credential unconstructible. Issue #8 correctly flagged this as a structural contradiction rather than an editorial one.

The pair is deliberate: the member-issued VMC is the member's consent artifact. A community can always issue a credential naming someone as a member, but it cannot produce the acknowledgement without that party's signature, so requiring both directions makes an unconsented membership claim unprovable. That rationale appeared nowhere in the text, which is why the contradiction was reachable in the first place.

So the prose was right and the schema was the defect. The two directions are now distinguished by issuer and subject rules rather than by a new credential type, matching how the VIC's two variants are handled.

- `spec/body.md`: VMC schema gains direction-qualified issuer/subject rules and a `digest` binding the acknowledgement to the grant, reusing the existing VWC digest algorithm verbatim; a second worked example; a new "Membership Edge Completion" subsection carrying the completeness, ordering and verifier rules plus the consent rationale; and a lifecycle editor's note deferring revocation to the planned Trust Task Protocols spec.
- `spec/body.md`: the per-direction witnessing rule generalised from VRCs to both edge-credential subtypes, so a witnessed membership edge has a defined `credentialSubject.id` binding.
- `spec/body.md`: new Security Consideration for unconsented membership assertion; "Digest integrity" extended to cover the VMC acknowledgement digest.
- `spec/terms-definitions/`: seven files corrected, including the "always ... C-DID" clause in `verifiable_membership_credential.md` that was the term-level source of the contradiction, and the CTA being "automatically" made a member without acknowledging.
- `CONTEXT.md`: VMC entry rewritten to describe both directions.

The verifier rule is deliberately direction-sensitive, which is the part worth reviewing closely: a member presenting their own community-issued VMC is accepted alone, since the act of presenting is itself the consent. A blanket "both always" would have broken the Community-Anchored ZKP and PHC constructions, which rely on the member holding only the community-issued half.

Resolves #8

title: Resolve the contradiction in VMC bidirectionality
body:
## Summary

The specification describes membership as a bidirectional graph edge formed by two Verifiable Membership Credentials, one in each direction. However, the normative VMC schema appears to permit only a community or network C-DID to issue a VMC to a member.

Under the current issuer and subject rules, it is not clear how the reverse-direction credential could be created.

## Detail

The specification indicates that:

* two VMCs, one in each direction, form a complete membership edge;
* the VMC issuer is the VTC or VTN C-DID; and
* the VMC subject is the member’s M-DID, or a VTC C-DID in the network-membership case.

A credential issued by the member to the community would therefore appear to violate the normative issuer rule.

This creates a structural inconsistency in the membership model rather than only an editorial ambiguity. Implementers cannot determine whether membership is:

* a unilateral community-issued assertion;
* a mutually issued credential pair;
* a community assertion plus member acceptance;
* or another form of bidirectional protocol state.

## Requested clarification

Please clarify what constitutes the reverse direction of the membership edge and specify the applicable issuer, subject and validation rules.

One possible resolution would be to model a VMC as a unilateral, community-issued membership assertion that creates a directed graph edge, while representing member acceptance or possession separately at the protocol or presentation layer.

Alternatively, if two credentials are required, the second credential and its semantics should be defined explicitly.

title: Specify both VMC directions so membership requires member consent (#12)
body:
Specify both VMC directions so membership requires member consent (#12)

* Specify both VMC directions so membership requires member consent

The spec asserted in five places that two VMCs form a complete
membership edge, but the normative schema required `issuer` to be the
VTC/VTN C-DID and the subject to be the member, making the reverse
credential unconstructible. Issue #8 correctly flagged this as a
structural contradiction rather than an editorial one.

The pair is deliberate: the member-issued VMC is the member's consent
artifact. A community can always issue a credential naming someone as a
member, but it cannot produce the acknowledgement without that party's
signature, so requiring both directions makes an unconsented membership
claim unprovable. That rationale appeared nowhere in the text, which is
why the contradiction was reachable in the first place.

So the prose was right and the schema was the defect. The two directions
are now distinguished by issuer and subject rules rather than by a new
credential type, matching how the VIC's two variants are handled.

- `spec/body.md`: VMC schema gains direction-qualified issuer/subject
  rules and a `digest` binding the acknowledgement to the grant, reusing
  the existing VWC digest algorithm verbatim; a second worked example;
  a new "Membership Edge Completion" subsection carrying the
  completeness, ordering and verifier rules plus the consent rationale;
  and a lifecycle editor's note deferring revocation to the planned
  Trust Task Protocols spec.
- `spec/body.md`: the per-direction witnessing rule generalised from
  VRCs to both edge-credential subtypes, so a witnessed membership edge
  has a defined `credentialSubject.id` binding.
- `spec/body.md`: new Security Consideration for unconsented membership
  assertion; "Digest integrity" extended to cover the VMC
  acknowledgement digest.
- `spec/terms-definitions/`: seven files corrected, including the
  "always ... C-DID" clause in `verifiable_membership_credential.md`
  that was the term-level source of the contradiction, and the CTA
  being "automatically" made a member without acknowledging.
- `CONTEXT.md`: VMC entry rewritten to describe both directions.

The verifier rule is deliberately direction-sensitive, which is the
part worth reviewing closely: a member presenting their own
community-issued VMC is accepted alone, since the act of presenting is
itself the consent. A blanket "both always" would have broken the
Community-Anchored ZKP and PHC constructions, which rely on the member
holding only the community-issued half.

Resolves #8

Signed-off-by: Geoff Turk <geoff@ic3.dev>

* Exclude the top-level proof from both digest computations

Both `digest` definitions — the new VMC one and the VWC one it copies
verbatim — specified the SHA-256 hash of "the credential's JSON
representation" canonicalized with JCS, without stating whether the
credential's top-level `proof` is part of that representation. Every
credential being hashed carries one, so two conforming implementations
could compute different values for the same credential.

That was latent in the VWC. This branch makes it reachable: a
member-issued VMC whose `digest` does not match "MUST NOT be treated as
completing a membership edge", so an unspecified canonicalization now
gates a normative MUST rather than only an attestation's strength.

Exclude the top-level `proof`. Both readings are defensible, but
excluding it binds the claims rather than one signed artifact, keeps
the digest stable across re-proofing, and stays well-defined for
unproofed forms. It also matches the choice the Trust Tasks framework
made in 0.5.0 (task digest excluding the top-level `proof`, step digest
including it), so a single verifier implementation stays valid across
both layers.

- `spec/body.md`: the exclusion clause added to the VMC and VWC
  `digest` definitions together — they are word-for-word copies, and
  clarifying only one would produce exactly the divergence at issue.
- `spec/body.md`: the "Digest integrity" security consideration's
  recompute rule matched to the definitions, so the verifier procedure
  and the schema agree on what is hashed.
- `spec/body.md`: Membership Edge Completion states the consequence —
  a re-signed grant with identical claims satisfies an existing
  acknowledgement, because the member's consent binds to the membership
  granted, not to a particular signature over it.

The `sha256:` + hex encoding is untouched; converting these to
`digestMultibase` is #17's scope, and this branch leaves it three sites
to convert rather than two.

Raised in review of #12 by Alberto Leon.

Signed-off-by: Geoff Turk <geoff@ic3.dev>

* Match the acknowledgement example to the did:webvh community DID

#20 moves the durable issuers in the examples from `did:web` to
`did:webvh`, including the community-issued VMC's `issuer`. It was cut
from `main` before this branch added the member-issued VMC, so it
updates the grant but not the acknowledgement that points back at it.

The two changes merge without a textual conflict — the lines are far
enough apart — leaving a member-issued VMC whose `credentialSubject.id`
is a different DID from the `issuer` of the grant it acknowledges. The
pair then no longer describes one membership edge, which is the only
thing that example pair exists to demonstrate, and no check in the
repository would catch it.

Point the acknowledgement at the same `did:webvh` value #20 uses for
the community, so the merged result is consistent.

This makes the branch depend on merge order: it is correct once #20 has
landed, and would itself introduce the mismatch, mirrored, if merged
first. Noted on both PRs.

Signed-off-by: Geoff Turk <geoff@ic3.dev>

* Bring the community-anchored ZKP's third statement under the consent rule

The direction-sensitive verifier rule exists so that requiring both
VMCs does not break the Community-Anchored ZKP and PHC. Review of #12
found it protects only part of the ZKP. Statement 2 picked up the
`community-issued` qualifier in 6bda431 and statement 3 did not, and
the carve-out was scoped to presentation by the subject of their own
membership. Statement 3 is neither: it is the holder asserting a
counterparty's membership on the strength of a community-issued VMC,
which is exactly the assertion the new MUST refuses without the
acknowledgement. The PR's own rationale said it meant to protect it.

Widening the carve-out from presentation to demonstration of possession
brings statement 2 inside it, since a possession statement in a proof
is not a presentation. It does not reach statement 3, whose prover is
not the subject and whose membership is not the prover's own; and the
consent property genuinely is at stake there, because a holder with a
real VRC from X could otherwise launder an unconsented grant naming X
into a "community-anchored" proof that X is a member.

What resolves statement 3 is provenance: whether the evidence came from
the counterparty or from the community. The artifact that carries the
counterparty's consent is their own member-issued VMC, which this
branch introduces. Whether the holder obtains it during the VRC
exchange belongs to the trust task protocol work, and how it is then
proven in zero knowledge belongs to the ZK protocol work; both are
already deferred. So the ZKP section now says what statement 3 rests
on, names the acknowledgement as the evidence that would satisfy the
rule, defers the mechanics, and gives verifiers an interim rule: treat
statement 3 as the community's attestation of the issuer's membership,
not as the issuer's acknowledgement of it. The MUST in Membership Edge
Completion points at that paragraph so it is not read as unconditional.

Also from the same review:

- `spec/body.md`: `digest` named as the direction discriminator where
  both endpoints are C-DIDs, since issuer/subject rules cannot classify
  a VTN-membership credential in hand.
- `spec/body.md`: the editor's note states the interim withdrawal
  controls. Because `digest` binds the acknowledgement to the grant's
  claims, a short `validUntil` on the grant forces re-acknowledgement
  by itself — a re-issued grant has a new digest the old
  acknowledgement no longer matches. A short window on the
  acknowledgement does something different: it bounds how long the
  community holds a presentable proof of consent.
- `spec/body.md`: new Privacy Consideration 7 for the acknowledgement
  as a transferable disclosure the community did not previously hold.
  #20 and #27 also add an item 7; whichever lands last renumbers.
- `spec/body.md`: PHC defined over the grant rather than "of a
  membership edge", and the review's question answered directly — an
  unacknowledged grant is a PHC for the member holding it, and the
  acknowledgement gates only the community's ability to assert it.
- `spec/body.md`: Security Consideration 3's "a VMC issuer being a
  recognized VTC" corrected for the acknowledgement, whose issuer is
  the member.

Raised in review of #12 by Brendan Miller.

Signed-off-by: Geoff Turk <geoff@ic3.dev>

Changelog

Sourced from jsonwebtoken's changelog.

11.0.0 (2026-07-24)

  • Add conversions between Algorithm and KeyAlgorithm
  • JWKs can now be created from DecodingKeys, creation from EncodingKey and DecodingKey now supports Ed25519 as well
  • JWKs with unknown key types are now deserializable
  • BREAKING: Algorithm, KeyAlgorithm, EllipticCurve and ThumbprintHash are now non_exhaustive
  • BREAKING: Jwk.thumbprint now returns a Result<_>
  • BREAKING: Header.extras is now a struct that allows for deserialization to any T
  • BREAKING: Implicit features resulting from optional crates have been removed
  • BREAKING: Validation.insecure_disable_signature_validation has been removed, use dangerous::insecure_decode instead
  • BREAKING: EncodingKey.inner has been renamed to as_bytes, try_get_hmac_secret has been removed
  • BREAKING: DecodingKey.as_bytes and try_get_hmac_secret have been removed, use try_get_as_bytes instead

Changes for CryptoProviders

  • When constructing HMAC signers, the algorithm family must now be verified on construction
  • JwkUtils has been renamed to KeyUtils
    • compute_digest now returns a Result<_>
    • extract_rsa_public_key_components has been renamed to rsa_pub_components_from_private_key
    • rsa_pub_components_from_public_key has been added
    • extract_ec_public_key_coordinates has been renamed to ec_pub_components_from_private_key
    • ed_pub_components_from_private_key has been added

Release notes

tower-http-0.7.0

Changes since 0.6.11

Added

  • csrf: add cross-site request forgery (CSRF) protection middleware, porting the cross-origin protection scheme introduced in Go 1.25 (#699)

    use tower::ServiceBuilder;
use tower_http::csrf::CsrfLayer;

    // Rejects cross-origin state-changing requests using Sec-Fetch-Site,
    
// an Origin allow-list, and an Origin/Host fallback. No per-request
    
// token state required.
    
let layer = CsrfLayer::new().add_trusted_origin("https://example.com")?;
    

    let service = ServiceBuilder::new().layer(layer).service_fn(handler);

  • timeout: add DeadlineBody for non-resetting body timeouts, applied via the new RequestBodyDeadlineLayer and ResponseBodyDeadlineLayer (#688)

    Unlike TimeoutBody, which resets its deadline on every frame, DeadlineBody caps the total time of a body transfer. A slow client trickling one byte at a time never trips an idle timeout but will trip a deadline.

    use std::time::Duration;
use tower::ServiceBuilder;
use tower_http::timeout::RequestBodyDeadlineLayer;

    // Abort the request body transfer after 30s total, regardless of how
    
// frequently data arrives.
    
let service = ServiceBuilder::new()
    
.layer(RequestBodyDeadlineLayer::new(Duration::from_secs(30)))
    
.service_fn(handler);

  • fs: add strong ETag support to ServeDir, including If-Match and If-None-Match precondition handling per RFC 9110. 304 Not Modified responses now carry the ETag and Last-Modified validators (#691)

  • fs: add a Backend trait to make ServeDir work with non-filesystem sources (e.g. embedded assets or object storage). The default TokioBackend preserves existing behavior. Use ServeDir::with_backend() to plug in custom implementations (#684)

    use tower_http::services::fs::ServeDir;

let service = ServeDir::with_backend("assets", MyBackend::new());

title: fix(ci): stop Dependabot emitting chore(deps)(deps) titles, and let a fixed title clear the check (#1172)
body:
fix(ci): stop Dependabot emitting chore(deps)(deps) titles, and let a fixed title clear the check (#1172)

* fix(ci): stop Dependabot emitting chore(deps)(deps) titles

`include: scope` appends the scope itself, so a prefix that already carries
one yields `chore(deps)(deps): bump …`. The commit-lint job checks the PR
title against the conventional-commit regex, which rejects it — so all six
cargo PRs Dependabot opened in the first hour were red on a check with
nothing to do with the bump.

The github-actions and docker entries were already correct: they set a
scoped prefix and do *not* set `include`, which is the other consistent
way to spell it.

Existing PRs are retitled by hand; the check reads the title, not the
branch's commit messages.

* fix(ci): let a fixed PR title actually clear the commit-lint check

`on: pull_request` with no `types:` defaults to opened/synchronize/reopened,
so an `edited` event never fires — and this check reads
`github.event.pull_request.title`. A PR whose only problem was its title
could therefore never go green by fixing the title: re-running the job
replays the original event payload, so it re-reads the old one, and the only
way out was to push a commit that changed nothing.

Five Dependabot PRs hit exactly that, which is how it surfaced.

Adding `edited` to ci.yml's trigger would re-run the docker builds, the
enclave build and the mobile build on every description tweak, so the job
moves to its own workflow instead: the one check that depends on PR metadata
is the one that reruns when PR metadata changes. The check name is unchanged,
so any branch-protection rule referencing it still matches, and nothing
`needs:` it.

title: feat(credentials)!: move vta/credentials/issue to 0.2 (#1159)
body:
feat(credentials)!: move vta/credentials/issue to 0.2 (#1159)

The last family behind its latest published spec. Checked against
`website/registry.json` rather than the schema files on disk: every other
implemented family is already on the newest published version.

0.1 and 0.2 have identical payloads. The response differs only in how it is
written — 0.2 composes it from `credentials/_shared/0.2`'s
`IssuedCredentialBase` instead of restating the members inline, which is
what stops the two drifting. The composition brings one new member,
`issuedAt`.

That member costs nothing to fill: `IssuedCredentialRecord` has carried
`issued_at` since the family existed, and 0.1 simply had nowhere to put it,
so the value was being computed, stored, and then dropped on the way out.
It stays `Option` on our side because the shared definition declares it
optional — a response without it is schema-valid and must still
deserialize — but the VTA always sends it.

The conformance sweep caught something on the way through, which is what it
is for. Its drifted-witness check asserts the generated type rejects an
unknown member, and 0.2's response type does not: closing a composed object
requires `unevaluatedProperties` (`additionalProperties` is evaluated
per-subschema and would reject the `allOf`-supplied members), and
trust-tasks-codegen maps only `additionalProperties: false` onto
`deny_unknown_fields`. So the generated struct is permissive where 0.1's
was strict.

The wire is unaffected — the schema itself is strict, so `validate_payload`
still rejects the member. What is lost is the type-level guard, which makes
the drifted-witness check pass vacuously. Recorded in
`PERMISSIVE_GENERATED_TYPE` with its reason and skipped rather than left to
give false assurance. The fix belongs in the codegen; deleting the entry
re-arms the check.

title: docs: a red semver report is the report working, not a defect to fix
body:
CLAUDE.md already says, in bold:

> **Never edit a `version = ` field in a feature PR.** Versions are assigned by the Release PR that release-plz maintains.

Three PRs did it anyway — #1156 (merged), #1159 and #1163 (since corrected). The rule was not unclear. What was missing is the inference between two documented facts:

- the check is named `semver report (informational — never blocks)`
- RELEASING.md says release-plz derives bump levels from the same tool

Neither says that a red result **on the PR that causes the break is the expected outcome**. So the red reads as a defect: bump the crate, watch it go green, conclude it was right.

This adds the sentence that closes that, and names the consequence — a manual bump isn't merely redundant work, it *collides* with the Release PR and fragments one coordinated release into several. #1163 proposed `vta-service` 0.21 → 0.22 while #1119 was already proposing exactly that, plus `vti-common` 0.14 → 0.15 covering a second finding I was about to chase in yet another PR.

Docs only.

title: Witness credentials are reasoned about but never built or verified
body:
## Summary

The ceremony engine treats `WitnessCredential` as a policy fact — with
trusted-issuer, validity and holder-binding predicates — but no VWC is ever
constructed or verified anywhere in the stack. `DTGCredential::new_vwc` and
`digest_multibase` are never called.

## Detail

`WitnessCredential` occurs in `ceremony/verify.rs`, `ceremony/facts.rs`,
`ceremony/evaluate.rs`, `routes/ceremonies.rs` and `policy/default.rs` — in
every case as a `credential_type` string in a fact the policy reasons over, not
as a credential the code builds or checks.

The exacting part is therefore entirely untested here. Per DTG Credentials the
VWC's `credentialSubject.digest` MUST be:

- the SHA-256 hash of the witnessed VRC,
- canonicalised with JCS (RFC 8785),
- encoded as a Multibase-encoded Multihash,
- `sha2-256` (header `0x12`, length `0x20`), base58btc (`z` prefix).

And Security Considerations 4 requires a verifier relying on that binding to
have the referenced VRC in hand, recompute the hash, and compare **decoded
digest bytes rather than encoded strings**.

`dtg-credentials` implements all of this correctly (`DTGCredential::digest`,
`digest_multibase`), including the recent multibase change. Nothing calls it.

## Why it matters

A ceremony can currently reach a decision on the *assertion* that a witness
credential was present, without any code path that could have established it
was valid or that it witnessed the edge in question. Security Considerations 4
is explicit that without recomputing the digest against the referenced VRC, a
VWC "should not be treated as evidence of which edge was witnessed".

## Suggested fix

1. Build VWCs through `new_vwc` on whatever path is meant to issue them.
2. On receipt, recompute the digest against the referenced VRC and compare
   decoded bytes.
3. `taskContext` is REQUIRED on the VWC specifically — see #1065, which is a
   prerequisite rather than a parallel task.

Conformance audit finding **F8**.

title: Pairwise relationship identifiers vs. the relationships ACL policy
body:
Raised from OpenVTC/openvtc#241, which proposes defaulting relationship
communication to pairwise Relationship DIDs (R-DIDs) rather than the persona
DID. That issue originates in an external RAHP/DRARM assessment finding
(`OVTC-RAHP-04`) scoring persona-DID relationship communication as stable-
identifier correlation.

The client-side half of that change is straightforward. But it collides with a
VTC policy, and the protocol question belongs here.

## The collision

`vtc-service/policies/default/relationships.rego` is the whole policy:

```rego
default allow := false
allow if {
	input.action == "publish"
	input.issuer_member.is_current
	input.subject_member.is_current
}
```

Both parties must be current, ACL-listed, non-tombstoned community members
(`vtc-service/src/routes/relationships.rs:122-134`, `:349-356`). And the issuer
is pinned to the authenticated session DID:

`vtc-service/src/routes/relationships.rs:97-107`
```rust
let issuer_did = extract_did_field(vrc, "issuer")?;
let subject_did = extract_subject_id(vrc)?;
if auth.did != issuer_did {
    return Err(AppError::Forbidden(format!(
        "session DID ({}) does not match VRC issuer ({issuer_did}) — \
         VRCs are self-issued; the VTC never mints them on a member's behalf", auth.did)));
}
```

A pairwise R-DID has no ACL row, so a VRC issued under one is rejected — 422
"subject DID … is not a current community member", or 403
`RelationshipPolicyDenied`. **The only enforcement that exists on this path
forbids pairwise identifiers rather than requiring them.**

`GET /v1/relationships/graph` (`routes/relationships.rs:446`) then deliberately
exposes the full correlatable member-to-member edge set to admins.

This is not a bug report — the ACL check is doing what it was designed to do.
It is a design question that the client cannot resolve on its own.

## The question

Should relationship communication use pairwise identifiers, and if so, how does
that reconcile with a trust graph whose entries are required to be attributable
to current members?

Some shapes worth weighing:

1. **Separate the two.** Pairwise identifiers govern the *communication channel*;
   the published VRC stays persona-attributed. This is roughly what OpenVTC does
   today — the R-DID carries post-handshake messages, the VRC `issuer` is the
   persona DID. It bounds the exposure to the graph, but the graph is exactly
   where the correlation the assessment describes lives.
2. **Pairwise in the graph, with a membership proof.** Let a VRC be issued under
   an R-DID accompanied by evidence that the R-DID belongs to a current member,
   without naming which. Costs a proof mechanism the stack does not have.
3. **Accept persona attribution as intended.** The trust graph's value may
   depend on edges being attributable; if so, say that explicitly so clients
   stop treating pairwise as an unrealised goal.

## What is currently true, for the record

The pairwise concept is absent from this repo and from `vta-sdk`. `pairwise`,
`R-DID` and `P-DID` do not appear as concepts; the word `pairwise` occurs once,
in an unrelated comment at `vtc-service/src/config.rs:764`. There is no
relationship protocol module in `vta-sdk` — the wire surface is four Trust Tasks
(`relationships/{list,graph,publish,revoke}/0.1`, `vtc-service/src/routes/mod.rs:631-644`),
and `PublishBody` is a single `vrc` field (`routes/relationships.rs:57`).
`vta-sdk` 0.27.0 → 0.28.0 changes nothing here.

Related prior decision: TSP relationship formation (the RFI/RFA invite→accept
FSM, and TSP's nested/pairwise VID APIs) was evaluated and dropped in favour of
relationship-free routed send —
`docs/05-design-notes/tsp-outbound-send.md:79-85`. Neither `form_relationship`
nor any nested-VID API is called anywhere in the repo.

The one "default to pairwise" statement in the design docs is
`design-docs/trust-task-delegation-architecture.md:278-285`, and it is scoped to
SIOPv2 / proxy-login subject DIDs against relying parties — not to relationship
edges.

## Why it matters more here than the generic pattern

The stable identifier in question is a published, resolvable `did:webvh` that
frequently carries a verified agent name. Two counterparties do not need traffic
analysis to correlate a persona across contexts — they compare a string and then
resolve it to a named identity. The linkage is a lookup, not an inference.

title: Structural issues in categorization of DTG credentials
body:
In reviewing @martipos PR https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec/pull/16, I realized we have an issue with spec as currently structured in Working Draft 01. 

We refer to "three functional categories" of DTG creds because at the proposal stage, we actually had three categories (with multiple members in each category). However, once we realized we only needed one verifiable invitation credential (VIC), we don't actually have three categories, only two:

1. Edge Credentials (VRCs and VMCs) 
2. Annotation Credentials (VWCs, VPCs, VECs)

Fixing this would also address the editorial issue that section "8. Invitation Credentials" currently only has just one subsection, "8.1. VIC (Verifiable Invitation Credential)". As a general rule, a spec should never have a section with only one subsection.

My proposed fix:

1. Move what is currently (in Working Draft 01) section "9. Annotation Credentials" to become the new section 8 (so it immediately follows section "7. Edge Credentials"). That way we cover the two categories of DTG credentials first in sections 7 and 8.
2. Change what is currently section "8. Invitation Credentials" to become the new section 9.
3. Change the name to "9. VIC (Verifiable Invitation Credential)".
4. Just include in section 9 the content of what is currently section 8.1.

title: fix(vtc): gate the fail-closed backend tests on the feature being absent
body:
`cargo test -p vtc-service --all-features` has been eight-red on every run, including on `main`:

```
failures:
    keys::seed_store::tests::aws_set_without_feature_is_config_error
    keys::seed_store::tests::azure_set_without_feature_is_config_error
    keys::seed_store::tests::config_secret_set_without_feature_is_config_error
    keys::seed_store::tests::explicit_aws_uncompiled_is_config_error
    keys::seed_store::tests::explicit_backend_uncompiled_is_config_error
    keys::seed_store::tests::gcp_set_without_feature_is_config_error
    keys::seed_store::tests::k8s_set_without_feature_is_config_error
    keys::seed_store::tests::vault_set_without_feature_is_config_error
```

Each asserts that a secret backend which is **not compiled** fails closed when its config field is set. Ungated they weren't merely redundant under `--all-features` — they were *guaranteed* to fail: with the feature compiled, `create_secret_store` correctly returns a store, and the test reads that as `expected a Config error, got a store (did the feature leak on?)`.

That's the sort of standing red that teaches people to skip the feature matrix — and the matrix is exactly where a fail-closed guard needs checking.

Each test now carries `#[cfg(not(feature = ...))]` for its own backend, matching the `#[cfg(feature = "vault-secrets")]` already on the compiled-side counterpart a few lines below. The gate is **per-backend** rather than one blanket `not(any(...))`: under `--features aws-secrets` only the aws case becomes unaskable, and the other five still have something to prove.

| build | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| default features | 13 pass | 12 pass |
| `--all-features` | 5 pass, **8 fail** | 5 pass |

`cargo test -p vtc-service --all-features` now reports no failures, and clippy is 0.

title: chore(vta)!: release vta-service 0.22.0 for the added ProvisionIntegrationOutput field
body:
The `semver report` is red on `main` again, with a different crate this time:

```
--- failure constructible_struct_adds_field ---
  field ProvisionIntegrationOutput.digest_multibase
    in vta-service/src/operations/provision_integration/mod.rs:178
Summary: semver requires new major version: 1 major and 0 minor checks failed
```

`ProvisionIntegrationOutput` gained `digest_multibase` with the provision/integration 0.3 cut-over while the crate stayed at 0.21.0. The struct is exhaustively constructible through the public API, so an existing literal no longer compiles.

Found because #1160 (which touches **no Rust at all** — it only adds `.github/dependabot.yml`) came back red on semver. A PR that changes no code failing a code check is how you know the finding is `main`'s, not the branch's.

This is the third of the same shape:

| PR | crate | cause |
|---|---|---|
| #1156 | `vta-sdk` 0.29 → 0.30 | `CreateKeyBody.key_id` added |
| #1159 | `vta-sdk` 0.30 → 0.31 | `IssueCredentialResponse.issued_at` added, `TASK_VTA_CREDENTIALS_ISSUE_0_1` renamed |
| this  | `vta-service` 0.21 → 0.22 | `ProvisionIntegrationOutput.digest_multibase` added |

That's the pattern, not a coincidence: the spec cut-overs add members and nothing bumps the crate carrying them. The semver report catches each one and is the only thing that does — worth remembering next time someone reads it as a broken check rather than a working one.

Bumps the crate and the single intra-workspace requirement that pins it (`vta-enclave`). `cargo check --workspace --all-features` is clean.

title: feat(vtc): verify the digest binding on a presented witness credential
body:
A VWC asserts that its issuer witnessed *one specific* relationship, and the only thing saying **which** is `credentialSubject.digest`. Nothing recomputed it.

The ceremony engine took `WitnessCredential` as a policy fact carrying trusted-issuer, validity and holder-binding predicates, and reasoned to a decision on the *assertion* that a witness was present — with no code path that could have established which edge, if any, it witnessed. DTG Credentials Security Considerations 4 is explicit that without recomputing the digest against the referenced VRC, a VWC "should not be treated as evidence of which edge was witnessed".

### The two decisions that are the substance

**Recomputed, not compared to the stored column.** `vrc_digest_multibase` is the right thing to *index* on and the wrong thing to *verify* against — it was written under whatever digest recipe was current when the row landed, and the rows still carry the migration note saying that form used to be bare lowercase hex over a recursive key sort. Comparing against it would assert that two stored strings agree, which isn't the claim being made.

The storage fixture stores a **deliberately wrong** column value for exactly this reason. An implementation that matched on the column passes every other test here and fails that one.

**Decoded bytes, not encoded strings.** Multibase is a *family* of encodings: the same 34-byte multihash is `z…` in base58btc and `f…` in base16. Two conforming implementations can assert the identical digest in strings that aren't equal, and a string comparison rejects an honest witness. It fails in the safe direction — which is precisely why it would have survived a long time undetected. There's a test for the cross-base case both as a unit and through storage.

### Where the verdict goes

To policy as a **fact**, not an enforcement decision — following `issuer_trusted` and the resolved `CredentialStatus`. The host does the work that needs storage; the policy branches on a settled state. A policy recomputing a digest would be a policy doing cryptography.

| variant | means |
|---|---|
| `Bound { relationshipId }` | the digest names an edge we hold — the only variant that establishes *which* |
| `Unresolved` | well-formed, but names no edge we hold |
| `Absent` | the credential asserts no digest |
| `Malformed` | present, but not a decodable `sha2-256` multihash |

Four variants because collapsing them loses what a verifier most needs. A witness naming an edge published on **another** VTC is `Unresolved`, not forgery — treating that as rejection refuses honest evidence, which is the same reason `CredentialStatus::Unknown` exists rather than a guess. `Malformed` stays separate because it can't be explained by an honest edge held elsewhere.

The raw-VP submit path records `None`, not `Unresolved`: that path verifies nothing, and `Unresolved` would claim it looked.

### Scope

This is **step 2** of the issue's suggested fix — verify on receipt. Two things it deliberately does not do:

- **Step 1, issuing VWCs through `new_vwc`,** needs the `taskContext` model in #1065, which the issue names as a prerequisite rather than a parallel task.
- **The personhood `assert` path** reads a different projection (`vp_claims.credentials`) and still allows on any `WitnessCredential` with a non-empty issuer, with no digest check. Same gap, different surface, untouched here.

14 tests, `cargo test -p vtc-service` green, clippy 0.

Refs #1068.

title: feat(vtc): verify the digest binding on a presented witness credential (#1161)
body:
feat(vtc): verify the digest binding on a presented witness credential (#1161)

A VWC asserts that its issuer witnessed one specific relationship, and the
only thing saying *which* is `credentialSubject.digest`. Nothing recomputed
it. The ceremony engine took `WitnessCredential` as a policy fact carrying
trusted-issuer, validity and holder-binding predicates and reasoned to a
decision on the assertion that a witness was present, with no code path that
could have established which edge — if any — it witnessed.

DTG Credentials Security Considerations 4 is explicit: without recomputing
the digest against the referenced VRC, a VWC "should not be treated as
evidence of which edge was witnessed".

`credentials::witness` recomputes it. Two decisions are the substance:

**Recomputed, not compared to the stored column.** `vrc_digest_multibase` is
the right thing to index on and the wrong thing to verify against — it was
written by whatever digest recipe was current when the row landed, and the
rows still carry the note saying that form used to be bare lowercase hex
over a recursive key sort. Comparing against it would assert that two stored
strings agree, which is not the claim. The test fixture stores a
deliberately wrong column value for exactly this reason: an implementation
that matched on it fails that test and passes every other one.

**Decoded bytes, not encoded strings.** Multibase is a family of encodings,
so the same 34-byte multihash is `z…` in base58btc and `f…` in base16. Two
conforming implementations can assert the identical digest in strings that
are not equal, and a string comparison rejects an honest witness. It fails
safe, which is why it would have survived a long time undetected.

The verdict reaches policy as a fact rather than an enforcement decision,
following `issuer_trusted` and the resolved `CredentialStatus`: the host
does the work needing storage, the policy branches on a settled state. Four
variants, because collapsing them loses what a verifier most needs — a
witness naming an edge held on another VTC is `Unresolved`, not forgery, and
a policy that cannot tell it from `Malformed` refuses honest evidence.

The raw-VP submit path records `None`, not `Unresolved`: that path verifies
nothing, and `Unresolved` would claim it looked.

Scope: this is step 2 of the issue's fix — verify on receipt. Step 1,
issuing VWCs through `new_vwc`, needs the `taskContext` model in #1065.
The personhood `assert` path reads a different projection and still accepts
any `WitnessCredential` with a non-empty issuer; that surface is untouched
here.

Refs #1068.

title: chore(ci): configure Dependabot version updates
body:
There is no `.github/dependabot.yml` in this repo at all.

Security *alerts* were already running — those are a repo-level default, and they're what surfaced the three `rustls-webpki` advisories fixed in #1158. What was missing is **version updates**: nothing proposed an ordinary bump, so the tree drifted until someone went looking. #1158 was that someone, by hand. The point of this file is that the next one is a pull request instead.

Three ecosystems, because the Rust tree isn't the whole artifact:

| ecosystem | cadence | why |
|---|---|---|
| `cargo` | weekly | the workspace; one manifest dir covers every member |
| `github-actions` | monthly | pinned majors in `ci.yml`, `docker.yml`, `publish.yml`, … |
| `docker` | monthly | `Dockerfile` + `Dockerfile.nitro` — a stale base is how a patched CVE misses the shipped container even when the crates are clean |

Grouping choices worth flagging:

- **Patch + minor grouped.** They're the bulk of the noise and rarely need reading individually; grouping keeps the majors legible.
- **AWS SDK grouped separately.** It releases as a set of ~10 crates that must move together — ungrouped, one week's bump is ten PRs that each fail to build alone.
- **Workspace crates ignored** (`vta-*`, `vti-*`, `vtc-*`). release-plz moves those; Dependabot would race it and propose bumps for crates #1119 is already moving.

`open-pull-requests-limit: 5` on cargo gives a normal week headroom without burying the queue. Security advisories aren't subject to that cap.

Note `dtolnay/rust-toolchain@master` and `taiki-e/install-action@cargo-semver-checks` are branch/tag refs Dependabot can't version — it leaves them alone, which is correct.

title: chore(deps): update dependencies and drop the legacy rustls tree
body:
Three parts.

### Lockfile refresh

`cargo update` moves 20 crates, including `trust-tasks-*` 0.17.0 → 0.17.1 and the `google-cloud-*` set.

### argon2 0.5 → 0.6

The only workspace requirement behind latest (`cargo outdated --root-deps-only` reports nothing else). `password_hash` 0.6 reworks what `claim_secret` used: `PasswordHash` moved to `password_hash::phc`, `SaltString` is gone because `hash_password` now draws its own salt from `getrandom`, and `Error::Password` is `Error::PasswordInvalid`.

Two upgrade risks the existing tests could not see, because every one of them hashes and verifies with the **same linked version** — both sides move together, so a format or derivation change passes silently:

| | why it survives an upgrade blind | now pinned by |
|---|---|---|
| Claim-secret PHC strings | persisted at invite-mint, read at claim time | a hash generated against 0.5, verified under 0.6 |
| Backup envelope KDF | envelope stores salt + params, not the key — so `hash_password_into`'s output *is* the format | a frozen vector, confirmed byte-identical across 0.5 and 0.6 |

A changed byte in the second would make every existing backup undecryptable, reported only as an AES-GCM tag failure. Both are verified, not assumed — the 0.5 fixtures were generated by building against 0.5 and comparing.

### The rustls-webpki advisories

All three open dependabot alerts (one **high**: DoS panic on a malformed CRL BIT STRING) are `rustls-webpki` 0.101, which has no fixed release in that line — the patched versions are 0.102.9+ / 0.103.

It arrived because `vti-secrets` took the AWS SDK's default features:

```
aws-sdk-secretsmanager feature "rustls"
  └── aws-smithy-runtime feature "tls-rustls"
      └── aws-smithy-http-client feature "legacy-rustls-ring"
          └── rustls 0.21 → rustls-webpki 0.101
```

`vta-tee` already pinned `default-https-client` explicitly; `vti-secrets` now does the same. That drops `h2`, `hyper` 0.14, `hyper-rustls` 0.24, `rustls` 0.21, `rustls-webpki` 0.101, `sct` and `tokio-rustls` 0.24 from the lockfile entirely. Nothing in the tree was using them — under default features it was lockfile-only, and under `--all-features` it was compiled but unused.

### Verification

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --tests` — 0
- `cargo test --workspace --all-features --exclude vtc-service` — green
- `cargo test -p vtc-service` — green

Note: `cargo test -p vtc-service --all-features` fails 8 `keys::seed_store` tests, and does so on `main` as well — they assert the cloud secret backends are *not* compiled ("did the feature leak on?"), which `--all-features` necessarily breaks. Pre-existing and out of scope here, but worth a follow-up to gate them.

title: fix(scripts): run the coverage suite with --all-features
body:
`scripts/trust-task-coverage.sh` builds the suite with the **default** feature set, so every `#![cfg(feature = ...)]` test binary is silently skipped. Neither `webvh` nor `transport-harness` is in `default`:

```
vta-service/tests/delegated_consent_e2e.rs:28:#![cfg(feature = "webvh")]
vta-service/tests/vault_release_didcomm.rs:14:#![cfg(feature = "transport-harness")]
```

so both binaries never run — the latter carrying `vault/{release,proxy-login,sign-trust-task}` — along with every `webvh`-gated test inside the binaries that do run.

The failure is invisible in the wrong direction. Nothing errors; the number is just too low, and the missing tasks read as harness gaps to go and write tests for that already exist. It cost a real afternoon: a `cargo test --all-features` run recorded the vault three, the script reported them uncovered, and the recorder looked at fault.

It matters on the report line too, not only the capture — the denominator comes from the dispatch table, which is itself feature-gated, so building the two halves with different feature sets compares a numerator and a denominator that don't describe the same service.

With this, and with #1154 and #1155 in front of it:

```
TRUST-TASK RESPONSE COVERAGE  109/109          (100%) — 0 never exercised
```

Stacked on #1155.
