title: fix(vta)!: re-case the extended error codes the Trust Tasks registry moved
body:
`trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#279` re-cased 200 extended error-code local
parts to lowerCamelCase per SPEC §4.10 rule 4 — `vault/upsert:version_conflict`
→ `vault/upsert:versionConflict`. Only the part after the `:` moved; the
namespace is unchanged. This repo still produced (and in one place read) the old
spelling for **32** of them.

Verified against `trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf@main` (543 declared codes
from `grep -rhoE 'code: …' specs --include=spec.md`). Every code below is
declared by the registry in the new spelling; only `did-management:unknownDomain`
is *also* still declared in the old one, and only by retired specs.

## Emitter vs matcher

The distinction governs every edit:

- **Emitter** — this repo decides what to send, and the registry decides what is
  correct to send. Moves to the new spelling, no compatibility arm.
- **Matcher** — this repo reads a code a peer produced, and cannot control that
  peer's deploy order. Accepts **both** spellings, with a `TODO` naming when the
  old arm can go.

**31 emitter codes, 1 matcher.** Commits are split so the two are reviewable
apart: `fix(vta)!` is the emitter side, `fix(vta-sdk)` is the matcher.

### Emitters (31 codes)

| Namespace | Local parts moved to camelCase |
|---|---|
| `auth/step-up/approve-response` | `acrUnsatisfied`, `approverUnauthorized`, `assertionInvalid`, `challengeExpired`, `challengeUnknown`, `noGate`, `subjectMismatch` |
| `device/heartbeat` | `notRegistered` |
| `device/register` | `alreadyRegistered`, `noPendingEnrolment` |
| `device/set-wake` | `notRegistered` |
| `did-management` | `unknownDomain` (prose only — see below) |
| `provision/integration` | `contextRequired` (`PROVISION_CONTEXT_REQUIRED`) |
| `task-consent/decision` | `noPending` |
| `vault/get` | `notFound` |
| `vault/proxy-login` | `credentialRejected`, `notFound`, `notProxyable`, `targetUnreachable` |
| `vault/release` | `notFound` |
| `vault/sign-trust-task` | `envelopeAlreadyProofed`, `envelopeExpired`, `envelopeInvalid`, `envelopeIssuerMismatch`, `notFound`, `notSignable` |
| `vault/upsert` | `contextChangeForbidden`, `envelopeUnsupported`, `notFound`, `sealedSecretInvalid`, `secretRequired`, `versionConflict` |

### Matcher (1)

`vta_sdk::agent_session::is_already_registered` reads
`device/register:alreadyRegistered` off whatever VTA the agent enrolled
against, so it now accepts both spellings. It matters more than its size
suggests: a missed match does not crash, it **falls open into a hard error** on
re-enrolment, and a smoke test that enrols once against a clean VTA never takes
the branch. `already_registered_accepts_both_registry_spellings` pins the
dual-accept as a property rather than trusting the comment beside it.

## ⚠️ Deploy order: the plugin PR must ship before this service

`PROVISION_CONTEXT_REQUIRED` now makes this service emit
`provision/integration:contextRequired`. `OpenVTC/vta-browser-plugin` matches
only the old spelling in users' browsers today — `onboard-view.tsx:307` gates
the onboarding context picker on an **exact equality**, so the picker would
silently stop appearing. A sibling change makes the plugin dual-accept.

**Ship the plugin PR, and let it reach users, before deploying this service.**

## Corrections to the code census

Two findings beyond the original list:

- **Three vault emitters build their namespace by interpolation**, so their
  codes appear as a literal nowhere and a flat grep misses them:
  `vault/{verb}:not_found` and `vault/{verb}:version_conflict`
  (`vault_not_found`, `check_expected_version`) and `vault/{op}:not_found`
  (`refuse_if_not_active`). Those helpers are what actually emit
  `vault/delete:notFound` and **`vault/delete:versionConflict`** — the code the
  census placed in the browser-plugin's set. It is emitted here too, and is
  fixed here.
- **`did-management:unknownDomain` splits 18 draft / 8 retired**, not 21/5. All
  eight snake_case declarations are `status: retired`; all eighteen camelCase
  ones are `status: draft`.

## How `did-management:unknown_domain` was handled

Both spellings are legitimately live, so the deciding question is which side
each site describes — and in this repo the answer is easy, because **there is no
emitter and no matcher for it here**. All eleven occurrences are prose.

- Ten describe register / publish / delete against a live hosting backplane.
  Their specs (`did-management/did/register`, `domain/assign`, and
  `did/publish`, which is retired and `supersededBy: did-management/did/register`)
  are draft and declare `unknownDomain`. Those move.
- The `CHANGELOG.md` entry is history and is left as written.

No dual-accept is needed for a code this repo neither sends nor reads.

## Deliberately not touched

Reported rather than changed:

- **`vault/credentials/*`** and the `LifecycleError::code()` tokens
  (`not_active`, `not_archived`, `already_deleted`, `not_deleted`,
  `grace_expired`) — the registry declares neither namespace in either casing.
  Re-casing them would invent a spelling rather than follow one.
- **Codes emitted into a registry namespace the registry does not declare them
  in** — `auth/step-up/approve-response:proof_invalid` (`step_up.rs:142`),
  `vault/proxy-login:{invalid_login_url,not_implemented,no_audience}`
  (`vault.rs:1671,1692,1959,1962`). A conforming consumer cannot branch on any
  of these. This is a spec gap, not a casing bug.
- **`vault/get` emits a bare `AppError::NotFound("vault entry {id} not found")`**
  (`vault.rs:706`) carrying no code at all, though the registry declares
  `vault/get:notFound`. Also a gap, and also out of scope here.
- **`password_post.rs:94-100`** writes `vault/proxy-login: credential_rejected`
  — namespace, *space*, token. Not a `ns:localPart` code, and the real emitter
  for that path is `password_post_error_to_reject` in `vault.rs`, which is
  fixed.
- **This repo's own vocabularies**: `auth:step_up_required`,
  `auth:consent_required`, `denied:no_pending`, `bbs:*`, `bootstrap:*`,
  `webauthn-vti-v1:*`, and the `not_registered` / `step_up_required` REST
  `error` fields on mediator drain-cancel (`protocol.rs:1218`,
  `api_integration.rs:3794`) and in `vtc-service`.

## Verification

Run with `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` inside the worktree, on the CI command set from
`.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` — clean
- `cargo build --workspace` — `Finished dev profile`, no warnings
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean
- `cargo test --workspace` — passing, **except two failures that predate this
  branch**: `vta-sdk --test client_rest` `get_did_webvh_returns_record` and
  `get_did_webvh_log_returns_log`, both `missing field \`record\``, fallout from
  the #1114 `dids/get` response fold. Reproduced identically on a detached
  `origin/main` with no changes applied.

title: fix(vta)!: re-case the extended error codes the Trust Tasks registry moved (#1122)
body:
fix(vta)!: re-case the extended error codes the Trust Tasks registry moved (#1122)

* fix(vta)!: emit the re-cased extended error codes the registry now declares

trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#279 re-cased 200 extended error-code local
parts to lowerCamelCase per SPEC §4.10 rule 4 — only the part after the `:`
moved, the namespace is unchanged. This service still produced the snake_case
spellings for 32 of them, so every one of those rejects carried a code the
registry no longer defines and no conforming consumer can branch on.

Every site here is an **emitter**: this repo decides what to send, and the
registry decides what is correct to send, so each moves to the new spelling
with no compatibility arm. The matcher side — where this repo reads a code a
peer produced and cannot control that peer's deploy order — is handled
separately in the following commit.

Three of the vault emitters build their namespace by interpolation
(`vault/{verb}:not_found`, `vault/{verb}:version_conflict`,
`vault/{op}:not_found` in `vault_not_found`, `check_expected_version` and
`refuse_if_not_active`), so the codes they produce do not appear as literals
anywhere. Those helpers cover `vault/delete:{notFound,versionConflict}` and the
`notFound` conflation the three consumer-facing use paths rely on for
enumeration resistance.

`did-management:unknownDomain` is declared twice over: 18 draft specs carry the
camelCase form and 8 retired ones are frozen at snake_case, so both spellings
are legitimately live. This repo has no emitter and no matcher for it — all
eleven occurrences are prose. Ten describe register / publish / delete against
a live hosting backplane, whose specs (`did-management/did/register`, and
`did/publish`'s successor, which is `did/register`) are draft, so they move to
`unknownDomain`; the CHANGELOG entry is history and is left as written.

Left alone deliberately: `vault/credentials/*` and the `LifecycleError::code()`
tokens (`not_active`, `already_deleted`, …), which the registry declares in
neither casing; `vault/proxy-login:{invalid_login_url,not_implemented}` and
`auth/step-up/approve-response:proof_invalid`, emitted into registry namespaces
the registry does not declare them in; and the `not_registered` /
`step_up_required` REST `error` fields, which are this service's own
vocabulary rather than Trust Task codes.

BREAKING CHANGE: reject reasons and problem-report codes for 32 extended error
codes across `auth/step-up/approve-response`, `device/{register,heartbeat,
set-wake}`, `provision/integration`, `task-consent/decision` and `vault/*` now
carry the lowerCamelCase local part. A consumer matching the snake_case
spelling on an exact comparison stops matching.

Refs #1059

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(vta-sdk): accept both spellings where the SDK reads a peer's error code

The emitter side of the #279 re-casing is settled by the registry: this repo
sends what the registry declares. The matcher side is not, because the code
arrives from whatever VTA the agent enrolled against and this SDK cannot
control that maintainer's deploy order. `is_already_registered` is the one such
site in the workspace — every other occurrence of a re-cased code here is
either an emitter or a fixture describing one.

It matters more than its size suggests. A missed match does not crash: it falls
open into a hard error on every re-enrolment, so the agent stops with an
enrolment failure against a VTA that is telling it, correctly, that it is
already enrolled. Nothing about that is visible to a smoke test, which enrols
once against a clean VTA and never takes this branch.

`already_registered_accepts_both_registry_spellings` pins the dual-accept as a
property rather than trusting the comment beside it, and the `TODO` names the
condition for dropping the old arm: one release after every VTA this SDK talks
to emits the re-cased code.

title: fix(vta)!: take keyId from the wire instead of minting one (#1123)
body:
fix(vta)!: take keyId from the wire instead of minting one (#1123)

First of the three stopgaps #1121 unblocked. `keys/create/0.1` publishes
`keyId` as of trust-tasks-rs 0.12.1 (dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#275), so the caller
names the key and the binding no longer has to invent one.

#1118 minted `internal-<uuid>` at the binding for an internal key. That was a
deliberate deviation from a SHOULD I wrote in #275 — a maintainer offering
internal keys and receiving no `keyId` SHOULD reject — taken because the
alternative was a security feature nobody could use: an internal key has no
derivation path to be named after, the operation layer refuses one without an
id, and the wire had no member to carry it. The comment at that site said to
delete it when the bump landed.

`VtaClient::create_key` also stops dropping `CreateKeyRequest::key_id`. That
was the third of the three fields #1118 found being dropped between the CLI and
the wire; the other two were fixed there and this one had nowhere to go.

The test now supplies `keyId` and asserts it comes back unchanged, alongside
the existing `origin == "internal"` check. The two answer different questions —
was the request honoured, and was the name I chose the name I got — and a
maintainer that silently renamed a key would pass the first.

BREAKING CHANGE: `CreateKeyBody` gains `key_id`. `keys/create/0.1` with
`internal: true` now requires the caller to supply `keyId`; the binding no
longer mints one.

title: fix(extension): accept both spellings of a re-cased error code
body:
Consumer-side follow-up to trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#279, which re-cased
~200 extended error codes to the lowerCamelCase that SPEC §4.10 rule 4 requires.
Only the local part after the `:` moved; namespaces are unchanged, and retired
specs were deliberately left snake_case and frozen.

## The defect

`onboard-view.tsx` gated the onboarding **context picker** on a `===` against
the old spelling:

```ts
res.code === "provision/integration:context_required" &&
```

Against a VTA that has taken #279, that comparison goes false — and then
*nothing else happens*. No error, no crash, no log line. The picker simply
stops appearing, and an operator with a multi-context VTA is dead-ended at
Connect, told a context is required and given no way to choose one. This is the
failure mode R3.7 exists to prevent, arriving through the front door: a real
machine-readable code, matched in a way that isn't stable.

## Why dual-accept, and not a swap

Swapping the literal would move the defect, not fix it.

This wallet is on the **matching** side of this wire and never the declaring
side — it reads codes an agent sends it. And it updates on the **Chrome Web
Store's** schedule while the VTA updates on **its own**:

| | against a pre-#279 VTA | against a post-#279 VTA |
|---|---|---|
| keep `context_required` | works | **picker never appears** |
| swap to `contextRequired` | **picker never appears** | works |
| accept both | works | works |

A wallet installed today still talks to a months-old agent next year; a wallet
that hasn't auto-updated meets an agent that took #279 this morning. **Both
halves of that fleet are live simultaneously**, so either literal alone is
correct for exactly half of it. Accepting both is the only spelling-independent
option — and it's the rule #124 already set for wire *field* names on the read
path ("emitting the canonical spelling and accepting either are separate
moves").

## The helper

`matchesTrustTaskCode(actual, canonical)` — new, in
`packages/core/src/trust-tasks/error-code.ts`, exported from the root barrel.

```ts
matchesTrustTaskCode(res.code, PROVISION_CONTEXT_REQUIRED)
// true for "provision/integration:contextRequired"
// true for "provision/integration:context_required"
```

Four properties are deliberate:

- **`canonical` is always the registry's current spelling.** Call sites read as
  the code declared *today*; the compatibility is confined to one module. That
  is what makes retiring the fold one edit rather than a sweep across ~200
  possible codes.
- **The snake_case form is derived, not a hand-maintained pair.** A drifted
  table looks exactly like no fold at all.
- **Only the local part is transformed.** #279 changed nothing before the `:`.
- **Not a fuzzy compare.** `contextRequired` and `contextNotFound` stay
  distinct, so a rename can't become a collision that surfaces the wrong
  recovery UX for a different rejection.

It carries a `// TODO:` naming the condition for dropping the snake_case arm: a
**declared** minimum vta-service floor at or above the release carrying the
re-cased codes — the way #125 made 0.18.0 a hard floor for the dispatcher path.
Until a floor is declared, an old agent is still a supported peer.

## Sites changed

**Matcher (behaviour):**

| site | change |
|---|---|
| `packages/extension/src/onboard-view.tsx` | `===` → `matchesTrustTaskCode(res.code, PROVISION_CONTEXT_REQUIRED)`; imports both from `@openvtc/pnm-core` |

**New:**

| site | change |
|---|---|
| `packages/core/src/trust-tasks/error-code.ts` | `matchesTrustTaskCode`, `trustTaskCodeSnakeCase` |
| `packages/core/src/trust-tasks/index.ts` | export the above |
| `packages/core/tests/trust-tasks.error-code.mjs` | 7 tests |

**Canonical constant:**

| site | change |
|---|---|
| `packages/core/src/provision/send.ts` | exports `PROVISION_CONTEXT_REQUIRED = "provision/integration:contextRequired"`, following the `MEDIATOR_REQUIRED` precedent in `bridge-protocol.ts`; the parse path documents that it passes the code through verbatim |
| `packages/core/src/provision/index.ts` | re-export |

**Message-passing path** — the code crosses offscreen → background → popup, and
is forwarded **verbatim at each hop**. Normalising in transit would make the
hops need redeploying in lockstep with the agent, and would hide from the popup
which side of the rename its peer is on. Both are documented so nobody
"helpfully" folds it upstream later:

| site | change |
|---|---|
| `packages/extension/src/bridge-protocol.ts` | `RuntimeOnboardConnectResponse.code` — re-spelled + verbatim-passthrough rationale |
| `packages/extension/src/offscreen.ts` | same, at the `ProvisionProblemReportError` catch |

**Doc comments naming the other three codes** — all three appear *only* in
prose, so there was nothing to fold, but they're now spelled as the registry
declares them with a pointer at the matcher, so the next site that starts
branching on one starts from the right shape:

| site | code |
|---|---|
| `packages/core/src/vault/delete.ts` | `vault/delete:versionConflict` |
| `packages/core/src/vault/sign-trust-task.ts` | `vault/sign-trust-task:notSignable` |
| `packages/core/src/vta/protocol.ts` | `vault/upsert:sealedSecretInvalid` |
| `packages/extension/src/onboard-view.tsx` | state comment above `contextCandidates` |

## Verified against the registry

All four re-cased codes confirmed against `dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf@main`
`specs/**/spec.md` (543 declared codes), not taken on trust:

```
provision/integration:contextRequired
vault/delete:versionConflict
vault/sign-trust-task:notSignable
vault/upsert:sealedSecretInvalid
```

## Left alone, deliberately

Swept every namespaced snake_case string in the repo. Three classes are
**correct as-is** and would be bugs to "fix":

- **`auth:consent_required`** (`vta/request-task.ts`) — a `details.reason`
  token, not an extended error code. The registry declares no bare `auth:`
  namespace at all, and the top-level `code` for this rejection is the
  framework's `taskFailed`. That file's own doc comment records that matching
  this against `code` is a defect the repo already had once.
- **`e.p.msg.context_required`** (`provision/run.ts`) — a DIDComm
  problem-report code. Different scheme, not governed by §4.10.
- **`push/register:bad_token`** (test fixture) — the registry still declares the
  whole `push/*` namespace in snake_case, and `bad_token` isn't declared at all;
  the test only asserts pass-through into an error string, with no matching.

No test fixtures, mock responses, string unions/enums or persisted state carry a
governed code. Persisted state was checked specifically: the only stored code is
the transient `contextCandidates` in React state within a single onboarding
attempt, so nothing can hold a stale spelling across sessions.

## Deploy order

**This must ship before the vta-service change that emits the new spelling.**
A sibling PR is updating `verifiable-trust-infrastructure` to emit
`contextRequired`; if that lands first, every wallet in the field loses the
context picker until it auto-updates. With this merged and released first, the
service-side rename needs no coordination at all — which is the whole point of
the fold, and why it's pinned by a test rather than by a comment.

## Verification

Real output, from a cold `npm ci` in a clean worktree:

- `npm run lint` (`tsc -b`, all four workspaces) — **clean**
- `npm run build` — **clean**, MV3 background bundle emitted at 48.16 kB
- `npm test` — **546 passing, 0 failing** (was 539; +7 here)
  - core 401, tsp-js 51, extension 85, reviewer-demo 9

Both CI-only guards re-run by hand against the built `dist/`:

- MV3 worker is a single self-contained bundle — no dynamic `import()` ✅
- No admin task URIs in the extension bundle ✅

Also confirmed the shipped bundle carries the canonical spelling
(`provision/integration:contextRequired` in `assets/send-*.js` and
`assets/options-*.js`) with the snake_case form derived at runtime rather than
duplicated as a literal.

### The seven tests

They pin the **property**, not the string manipulation:

- both spellings match, for all four re-cased codes
- the snake_case form is derived, so it can't drift
- only the local part is re-cased; the namespace is untouched
- a different code in the same namespace does **not** match
- the namespace is part of the identity (`vault/upsert:versionConflict` ≠
  `vault/delete:versionConflict` — both are real codes with the same local part)
- absent/empty `code` is not a match — a transport failure carries no
  problem-report, and mistaking that for the one code we act on would open the
  picker on a network blip
- the exported constant is in the registry's current spelling

## Checklist (stack guide §9)

- [x] No new bare `fetch()`; no network code touched (R1.2)
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3)
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect (R2.1)
- [x] Every retry bounded + backed off (R1.4)
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5)
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6)
- [x] **Errors matched on stable machine-readable codes, never strings
      (R3.7)** — the whole PR; the match is now stable across the registry's
      re-casing rather than pinned to one side of it
- [x] **Contract change coordinated with the Rust side, not guessed (R3.6)** —
      verified against the registry's declarations and sequenced ahead of the
      service-side emit
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive (R5.*) — an absent code matches nothing
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified (R6.*)
- [x] Deviations flagged with rule numbers

title: chore(deps)!: trust-tasks-rs 0.12 and the TDK crates that carry it
body:
Moves the workspace to `trust-tasks-rs` **0.12**, now that
[affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs#743](https://github.com/affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs/pull/743)
has published the messaging crates that carry it. This was the blocker on three
separate pieces of work.

## Everything moves together, because two nodes do not compile

| dependency | from | to |
|---|---|---|
| `trust-tasks-rs` | 0.11.17 | **0.12** |
| `trust-tasks-capability-client` | 0.10 | 0.11 |
| `trust-tasks-https` | 0.10 | 0.12 |
| `trust-tasks-didcomm` | 0.10 | 0.12 |
| `trust-tasks-proof` | 0.10 | 0.11 |
| `affinidi-tdk` | 0.8.5 | 0.9 |
| `affinidi-messaging-sdk` | 0.19 | 0.20 |
| `affinidi-messaging-test-mediator` | 0.2 | 0.3 |

These are one change, not eight. `trust-tasks-rs` types reach the public API of
each — `affinidi-messaging-sdk`'s `account_update` takes an
`account::update::v0_1::MediatorAcl` — so a graph holding two versions fails to
compile rather than warn:

```
error[E0308]: mismatched types
   --> vta-sdk/src/acl_setup.rs:147:18
    |                  ^^^ expected `MediatorAcl`, found a different `MediatorAcl`
```

`cargo tree -i trust-tasks-rs` now returns a single node at 0.12.1.

A fourth pin lived in `tests/e2e/Cargo.toml` and is easy to miss: the workspace
resolved clean without it while that crate quietly held
`affinidi-messaging-test-mediator 0.2` — and through it the whole 0.11 chain.

## One source change

`classify_git_trust_reply` gained a required `expected_thread_id` in
capability-client 0.11. The reason is in its own docs: acting on an
uncorrelated reply means "letting whichever document arrives next decide the
fate of a write it has nothing to do with."

`DidcommCapabilityWriter` already registers its waiter on `doc.id`, so this is
defence in depth rather than a live bug — and `correlation_thread` is the
library's own SPEC §4.9 rule (`threadId`, falling back to `id`) rather than
this call site's guess at it.

## Verified before the crates published

The whole chain was checked against a path `[patch.crates-io]` over the TDK
workspace before #743 merged, so the move was known to work rather than hoped
to. This branch has since been re-resolved against the real registry and gives
the same result.

## What this unblocks

Three stopgaps, each of which names this bump at its own site, now become
deletions — deliberately **not** done here, so this change is a dependency move
and nothing else:

- the hand-rolled freshness bounds from #1117, in favour of `FreshnessPolicy` /
  `TrustTask::validate_freshness` (same two rules, same 60s skew, plus the
  `max_age` window);
- the minted `key_id` branch from #1118, in favour of the wire `keyId` that
  `trust-tasks-rs` 0.12.1 publishes;
- this workspace's `replay::check_and_record`, in favour of `ReplayGuard`.

## Gates

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --features vta-service/test-support -- -D warnings`
- `./scripts/trust-task-coverage.sh` — 28 suites green, **0 violations**, coverage 48/109 unchanged
- `cargo fmt --all --check`

Refs #1059

title: docs(specs): re-case references to the §8.3 standard error codes (SPEC §4.10 rule 2, a MUST)
body:
## This is rule 2 (MUST), not rule 4 (SHOULD)

SPEC §4.10 draws a line that PR #279 stayed on one side of, and this PR closes the other.

| | Rule 4 — #279 | Rule 2 — this PR |
|---|---|---|
| Strength | **SHOULD** | **MUST** |
| Governs | values a *specification* defines for itself | values *the framework* defines |
| Here | ~200 extended `code` local parts | 28 references to the §8.3 standard codes |

> **Rule 2.** Enumerated string values defined by this framework — notably the standard error `code` identifiers of [§8.3] — **MUST** be expressed in **lowerCamelCase**.

#279 said in as many words that it was leaving these: *"References to framework standard codes and to codes declared nowhere are left as they are; both are separate defects."* This is the first of those two. The second is reported at the bottom, not fixed.

There is also a non-taste argument that settles every site in scope: each one cites `/SPEC.md#83-standard-error-codes`, and that table has not contained the snake_case spelling since framework 0.2 re-cased it. The prose names a code its own citation does not contain — precisely the broken cross-reference #280 fixed for extended codes.

## What changed

28 occurrences across 18 files. All `status: draft`, re-confirmed per file, so §5.2's within-draft rule applies and **requires** the fix in place, errata-style, with no new version.

**`permission_denied` → `permissionDenied`** — 24 in 14 files
`acl/change-role/0.1`, `acl/grant/0.1` (×2), `acl/list/0.1`, `acl/revoke/0.1`, `acl/show/0.1` (×2), `auth/passkey/login/start/0.1`, `keys/create/0.1` (×2), `keys/derive-and-sign/0.1` (×2), `keys/derive-and-sign-document/0.1` (×2), `keys/import/0.1` (×2), `keys/rename/0.1` (×2), `keys/revoke/0.1` (×2), `keys/show/0.1` (×2), `keys/sign/0.1` (×2)

**`proof_invalid` → `proofInvalid`** — 2 in 2 files
`auth/step-up/approve-response/0.1`, `vault/sign-trust-task/0.1`

**`malformed_request` → `malformedRequest`** — 2 in 2 files
`did-management/_shared/0.1/CONVENTIONS.md`, `trust-task-discovery/0.1/payload.schema.json` (a schema `description`)

Every occurrence was classified before being touched. None is a declared extended code — verified against each spec's `errorCodes` front matter — and none is prose that merely resembles a code.

## `trust-task-error/0.1` is **not** re-cased, and that is the load-bearing decision

It holds 25 snake_case occurrences and is the file this change most obviously points at. It is the one file that must not move, and the brief for this work assumed the opposite, so the reasoning is worth stating in full.

That spec does not *reference* the §8.3 codes. It **defines** them. Its payload schema `enum` is the published framework-0.1 error vocabulary, and `trust-task-error/0.2` was minted for the sole purpose of carrying the re-cased set:

```console
$ diff specs/trust-task-error/0.1/payload.schema.json specs/trust-task-error/0.2/payload.schema.json
```

returns `$id`, those ten code spellings, and the extended-code pattern. Nothing else. Four independent things in this repo say to leave it alone:

1. **SPEC Appendix B**, on the framework-0.2 re-casing: *"the snake_case `0.1` codes remain valid for documents whose `type` resolves to a `0.1` specification."*
2. **`trust-task-error/0.2` declares `wireCompatibleWith: "0.1"`** — the field §5.2 defines so that *"consumers can dual-accept documents of the predecessor by mechanical normalization."* Re-casing the predecessor deletes the thing consumers are told to normalize and leaves 0.2 with no reason to exist.
3. **`spec.meta.schema.json`** already describes the 0.1 casing as *"frozen 0.1 snake_case"* and accepts both casings deliberately so 0.1 and 0.2 validate against one schema.
4. **`build-registry.mjs`'s own comment** on the `wireCompatibleWith` integrity check calls the promise *"dual-accept 0.1 by re-casing and retyping"* — the re-casing happens in the consumer, at read time, not in the registry.

§5.2's in-place draft rule is scoped to changes carrying *"no semantic difference on the wire."* This one **is** the wire difference. Re-casing it would invalidate already-issued 0.1 documents, which is the same harm §5.3 protects retired specs from — the status differs, the wire consequence does not.

Also untouched: `spec.meta.schema.json`'s `'acl/grant:permission_denied'` example. It is a *namespaced extended* code illustrating the frozen spelling the pattern still accepts — §8.5 and rule 4 territory, not rule 2's.

## The lint

`scripts/lib/error-code-casing.mjs` gains a companion, `checkStandardErrorCodeCasing()`, wired into `build-registry.mjs` beside the rule-4 report.

The existing lint **could not** have caught these, structurally rather than by oversight: it reads `errorCodes` front matter, because that is where an extended code is *declared*. A standard code is declared nowhere — it belongs to the framework and appears in a spec only as a reference, in prose, in a `description`, in an example. So the companion sweeps the text of every `.md` and `.json` under `specs/`. (#280 exists because the rule-4 lint reads declarations and could not see prose; this one is built the other way round from the start.)

Following #279's shape: hard failure, no allowlist file, exemptions derived from front matter and counted every build.

```
  Error code casing: 682/730 extended code(s) are lowerCamelCase; 48 frozen in 15 retired spec(s) (§5.3 — exempt, not debt), 0 non-conforming
  Standard error code casing: 1024 spec file(s) swept for §8.3 codes; 25 snake_case occurrence(s) frozen in 1 superseded/retired spec(s) (§5.2/§5.3 — exempt, not debt), 0 non-conforming
```

Two exemptions, both read off disk:

1. **`status: retired`** (§5.3) — identical reasoning to the rule-4 lint.
2. **The superseded spelling of the framework error vocabulary itself**, requiring *both*: the version's own payload schema carries an `enum` that IS the §8.3 vocabulary (≥3 standard codes in one closed set — only `trust-task-error/*` does this), **and** a later version of the same slug declares `wireCompatibleWith` naming it.

The second half of (2) is what keeps the first half honest: a spec that merely invents a snake_case enum gets nothing, only one a successor has formally declared it has normalized away. That exempts `trust-task-error/0.1` without an allowlist naming it.

**Verified both directions.** Re-injecting `permission_denied` into `acl/revoke/0.1` → exit 1 naming file, line, rule and conforming spelling. Injecting `task_failed` into `trust-task-error/0.2` — which defines the vocabulary but that no successor points at — → exit 1, while 0.1 stayed exempt at 25.

## Checks

| | |
|---|---|
| `npm run validate` | ✅ 349 specs, 65 shared schemas |
| `npm run build` | ✅ exit 0 |
| `npm run check-bindings` | ✅ 349 specs vs 349 TS and 344 Rust modules — all agree |

**Bindings drifted**, in one spec only. `trust-task-discovery/0.1`'s `requiredExt` description named `malformed_request`, and the generators embed `payload.schema.json` verbatim. Regenerated via `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen && cargo fmt --all` and `npm run build-ts-bindings`; the movement is confined to doc comments and the embedded `PAYLOAD_SCHEMA` literal in `specs::trust_task_discovery::v0_1` and `trust-task-discovery/0.1/payload.ts`. Descriptions do not participate in validation — no type, constant or behaviour change, so a patch:

```
trust-tasks-rs        0.13.1 -> 0.13.2   (+ CHANGELOG)
@openvtc/trust-tasks  0.14.1 -> 0.14.2
```

---

# Reported, not fixed — two follow-ups

Both surfaced while classifying the scope above. Each is a semantic change, not a casing fix, and wants its own PR.

## 1. 93 specs re-declare a §8.3 standard code under their own namespace

Larger than the ~90 figure suggested, and the shape is worse than redundancy — **§8.5 forbids it outright**: *"Extended codes **MUST NOT** shadow any code listed in §8.3."* So these are MUST violations too, of a different rule.

**95 declarations across 93 specs:**

| local part | count |
|---|---|
| `permissionDenied` | 90 |
| `expired` | 2 |
| `idConflict` | 2 |
| `identityMismatch` | 1 |

By status: 91 draft, 4 retired (the retired ones are frozen by §5.3 and stay).

The non-`permissionDenied` five, since they are easy to miss in a sweep aimed at the big number:

- `credential-exchange/pending/approve/0.1` → `credential-exchange/pending/approve:expired`
- `task-consent/request/0.1` → `task-consent/request:expired`
- `vta/contexts/create/1.0` → `vta/contexts/create:idConflict`
- `vta/webvh/servers/register/1.0` → `vta/webvh/servers/register:idConflict`
- `vtc/backup/import/0.1` → `vtc/backup/import:identityMismatch`

**The redundancy claim holds under checking.** Across `trust-tasks-rs`, `trust-tasks-ts` and the binding crates, the namespaced form appears in exactly three places, all of them unit-test assertions exercising the family-namespace *string helper* rather than consuming any spec's declaration:

```
trust-tasks-rs/src/payload.rs:279   assert_eq!(code.to_string(), "acl:permissionDenied");
trust-tasks-rs/src/payload.rs:316   assert_eq!(code.to_string(), "acl:permissionDenied");
trust-tasks-ts/test/codes.test.ts:109  familyCode(GRANT_RESPONSE, "acl", "permissionDenied")
```

Note those say `acl:`, a *family* namespace, not any of the 90 `<slug>:` forms actually declared. Meanwhile 17 source files across both SDKs use the bare standard `permissionDenied`. Nothing consumes the namespaced declarations.

Why it needs its own PR: removing a declared code changes what a spec says it can emit. It is a §8.5 conformance fix with a migration story for any emitter sending the namespaced spelling, not a re-casing. Worth noting that `checkErrorCodeNamespaces()` already validates the *prefix relationship* of a namespace but never asks whether the local part shadows §8.3 — the check is one condition short, and that is probably where the fix belongs.

## 2. `keys/*` specs name codes they never declare — a §8.5 namespacing defect

**All nine** `keys/*` specs declare `errorCodes: []`. **Seven** of them name codes in prose anyway (the brief said 8; `keys/list/0.1` and `keys/show/0.1` declare nothing and name nothing beyond the standard `permission_denied` this PR re-cased, so the count is seven):

| spec | codes named in prose, declared nowhere |
|---|---|
| `keys/create/0.1` | `already_exists`, `invalid_argument` |
| `keys/derive-and-sign/0.1` | `invalid_argument` |
| `keys/derive-and-sign-document/0.1` | `invalid_argument` |
| `keys/import/0.1` | `already_exists`, `invalid_argument` |
| `keys/rename/0.1` | `not_found`, `already_exists` |
| `keys/revoke/0.1` | `not_found` |
| `keys/sign/0.1` | `invalid_argument`, `failed_precondition` |

Four distinct codes: `not_found`, `already_exists`, `invalid_argument`, `failed_precondition` — note `failed_precondition`, which the brief did not list.

None appears in §8.3, so none is a standard code and rule 2 does not reach them. None is declared, so none is an extended code either. They are named in normative sentences — *"Failures (`permission_denied`, `not_found`) use `trust-task-error`"* — which makes them codes a consumer is told to expect and a producer cannot look up. That is a §8.5 defect (an extended code MUST be namespaced and, per §7.3 item 9, declared with its meaning, default `retryable`, and `details` schema), and it is also why they are wire-unreachable: `trust-task-error`'s `code` pattern requires a namespace, so a bare `not_found` will not validate.

They were deliberately left in snake_case here. Re-casing them to `notFound` would produce a tidy-looking corpus of codes that are still undeclared, unnamespaced and unvalidatable — papering over the defect rather than fixing it. The fix is to declare them as `keys:<local>` (a family namespace covering all nine, since these are family-wide conditions §8.5 explicitly permits naming once) with the front matter §7.3 item 9 requires, and re-case in the same change.

For scale, `errorCodes: []` is declared by 43 of 349 specs registry-wide; `keys/*` is the cluster where prose and declaration visibly disagree.

title: docs(specs): re-case references to the §8.3 standard error codes (SPEC §4.10 rule 2, a MUST) (#281)
body:
docs(specs): re-case references to the §8.3 standard error codes (SPEC §4.10 rule 2, a MUST) (#281)

* docs(specs): re-case 28 references to the §8.3 standard error codes per SPEC §4.10 rule 2

SPEC §4.10 draws a line PR #279 stayed on one side of. Rule 4 is a SHOULD over
values a specification defines for itself, which is what #279 fixed for ~200
extended codes. Rule 2 is a MUST over values the framework defines:

  "Enumerated string values defined by this framework — notably the standard
   error `code` identifiers of §8.3 — MUST be expressed in lowerCamelCase."

#279 said so explicitly and left them: "References to framework standard codes
and to codes declared nowhere are left as they are; both are separate defects."
This is the first of those two.

28 occurrences across 18 files, all `status: draft`, so §5.2's within-draft rule
applies and requires the fix in place, errata-style, with no new version:

  permission_denied -> permissionDenied   24 in 14 files
    acl/{change-role,grant,list,revoke,show}/0.1
    auth/passkey/login/start/0.1
    keys/{create,derive-and-sign,derive-and-sign-document,import,
          rename,revoke,show,sign}/0.1
  proof_invalid     -> proofInvalid        2 in 2 files
    auth/step-up/approve-response/0.1, vault/sign-trust-task/0.1
  malformed_request -> malformedRequest    2 in 2 files
    did-management/_shared/0.1/CONVENTIONS.md
    trust-task-discovery/0.1/payload.schema.json (a schema `description`)

Every one of these is also a broken cross-reference, which is what makes the
call unambiguous rather than a matter of taste: each site cites
/SPEC.md#83-standard-error-codes, and that table has not carried the snake_case
spelling since framework 0.2 re-cased it. The prose names a code its own
citation does not contain — the same defect #280 fixed for extended codes.

Not touched, deliberately:

* `trust-task-error/0.1` — 25 occurrences, and the one file that looks most
  like the point of this change. It is the opposite. That spec does not
  *reference* the §8.3 codes, it *defines* them: its payload schema enum is the
  published framework-0.1 error vocabulary. `trust-task-error/0.2` was minted
  for the sole purpose of carrying the re-cased set — diff the two payload
  schemas and the only differences are `$id`, those ten spellings, and the
  extended-code pattern — and 0.2 declares `wireCompatibleWith: "0.1"`, the
  field §5.2 defines so "consumers can dual-accept documents of the predecessor
  by mechanical normalization". SPEC Appendix B is explicit: "the snake_case 0.1
  codes remain valid for documents whose `type` resolves to a 0.1
  specification". Re-casing 0.1 would invalidate already-issued 0.1 documents,
  delete the thing consumers are told to normalize, and leave 0.2 with no
  reason to exist. §5.2's in-place rule is scoped to changes that carry "no
  semantic difference on the wire"; this one is the wire difference.

* `specs/spec.meta.schema.json` — its `code` description gives
  'acl/grant:permission_denied' as an example of the frozen 0.1 spelling the
  pattern still accepts. That is a *namespaced extended* code, which is §8.5 and
  rule 4 territory, not rule 2's, and the example is doing deliberate work.

* Bare `not_found` / `already_exists` / `invalid_argument` /
  `failed_precondition` in seven keys/* specs. None is a §8.3 code, so rule 2
  does not reach them; they are undeclared codes under §8.5 and re-casing them
  would paper over that. Reported on the pull request instead.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* chore(specs): fail the build on a §8.3 standard error code written in snake_case

The rename in the previous commit is only half the work, exactly as it was in
#279. Nothing enforced §4.10 rule 2, which is how 28 references to the standard
codes sat in the registry citing a §8.3 table that stopped containing those
spellings at framework 0.2.

The rule-4 lint added by #279 could not have caught them, and the reason is
structural rather than an oversight. It reads `errorCodes` front matter, because
that is where an *extended* code is declared. A *standard* code is declared
nowhere — it belongs to the framework and appears in a specification only as a
reference, in prose, in a schema `description`, in an example. So this companion
sweeps the text of every .md and .json file under specs/ instead. (#280 exists
because the rule-4 lint reads declarations and could not see prose; this one is
built the other way round from the start.)

Only ten of the fourteen §8.3 codes can be miscased — `expired`, `cancelled`,
`unavailable` and the like are single words. A match preceded by `:` is ignored:
`acl/grant:permission_denied` is a namespaced extended code, which is rule 4's
business. (§8.5 does forbid an extended code from shadowing a standard one, but
that is a namespacing question for checkErrorCodeNamespaces, not a casing one.)

Following the shape #279 established: a hard failure rather than a warning
behind an allowlist, because the corpus was taken to zero in the commit before
this one — and because rule 2 is a MUST, so a warning would be the wrong
strength even if the corpus were dirty. No allowlist file. Both exemptions are
derived from what is on disk and counted on every build:

  1. `status: retired` (§5.3) — same reasoning as the rule-4 lint.

  2. The superseded spelling of the framework error vocabulary itself, which
     needs *both* of: the version's own payload schema carries an enum that IS
     the §8.3 vocabulary (three or more standard codes in one closed set — only
     trust-task-error/* does this, being the spec that defines the codes rather
     than citing them), AND a later version of the same slug declares
     `wireCompatibleWith` naming it.

Condition 2 is what exempts trust-task-error/0.1 without naming it. The second
half is what keeps the first half honest: a spec that merely invents a
snake_case enum of its own gets nothing, only one a successor has formally
declared it has normalized away. Verified by injecting `task_failed` into
trust-task-error/0.2 — which defines the vocabulary but that no successor points
at — and watching the build fail on it while 0.1 stayed exempt.

  Standard error code casing: 1024 spec file(s) swept for §8.3 codes;
  25 snake_case occurrence(s) frozen in 1 superseded/retired spec(s)
  (§5.2/§5.3 — exempt, not debt), 0 non-conforming

The frozen count behaves like #279's: it can only shrink. `retired` is terminal,
and an entry leaves the second exemption only when a `wireCompatibleWith`
declaration is withdrawn or the spec is deleted. If it rises, something has
re-published a frozen artifact and the build log says so.

Also verified by re-injecting `permission_denied` into acl/revoke/0.1: exit 1,
naming the file, the line, the rule, and the conforming spelling.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* chore(release): regenerate bindings after the standard error code re-casing

The generators embed payload.schema.json verbatim, so a code named inside a
schema `description` drifts the generated modules. Exactly one schema did:
trust-task-discovery/0.1, whose `requiredExt` description said a producer
"will receive a `malformed_request` rejection".

The movement is confined to that one spec's two generated modules, and within
them to description text and the embedded PAYLOAD_SCHEMA literal. Descriptions
do not participate in validation, so no generated type, constant or behaviour
changes — a patch on both libraries, on the same reasoning as 0.13.1.

  trust-tasks-rs        0.13.1 -> 0.13.2
  @openvtc/trust-tasks  0.14.1 -> 0.14.2

Nothing moved on trust-task-error's account, and would not have even if that
spec had been re-cased: it is in the codegen's SKIP_SLUGS, with the Rust side
hand-modelled in error.rs.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

---------

title: test(vta): cover the contexts, app-state and memory families
body:
Takes the VTA's Trust Task response coverage from **34/109 to 48/109 (31% →
44%)** — three test functions covering fourteen tasks. Zero violations, zero
failures.

## Why coverage, again

The conformance gate validates real handler output, so it is evidence only
about tasks a test actually exercises. Every previous batch found a defect the
moment it looked: covering `keys/{show,sign,…}` immediately surfaced
`contextId: null` on the shared `KeyRecord`, which six tasks return.

This batch found none, which is also worth recording — `vta/contexts/*`,
`vta/app-state/*` and `vta/memory/*` were already conformant.

## What is covered

| family | tasks |
|---|---|
| `vta/contexts/*` | `create`, `list`, `get`, `update`, `preview-delete`, `delete` |
| `vta/app-state/*` | `put`, `get`, `list`, `put-many`, `get-many`, `delete` |
| `vta/memory/*` | `put`, `list`, `delete` |

Each test walks a lifecycle rather than poking one endpoint, so the reads see
state a write actually made — a `get` against an empty store exercises the
not-found path, not the response shape this gate is about. `preview-delete` is
covered immediately before `delete` because that pair exists so an operator can
see what a delete would take with it.

## Why `vault/{release,proxy-login,sign-trust-task}` are still uncovered

Worth stating, because it explains a shape in the remaining 61.

`vault_trust_task.rs` already has tests named `*_reaches_handler_past_gate` for
all three. They deliberately name a **missing** entry: their subject is gate
ordering, so they assert on a reject and never produce a success document.
That is correct for what they test, and it is exactly why the gate has never
seen these tasks.

I tried to add success paths and hit a real constraint rather than a gap in the
tests: `vault/release` seals its secret into a DIDComm envelope, so it fails in
the unit fixture with *"ATM not configured — server cannot pack DIDComm
envelopes"*. Covering it needs the mediator-backed `transport-harness`, which
is its own change. `vault/release/0.1` is also deprecated in favour of `0.2`,
so the coverage is better spent on the successor.

So the remaining 61 are not uniformly cheap: some are one lifecycle test like
these, and some need real transport infrastructure standing up.

## Gates

- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --features vta-service/test-support -- -D warnings`
- `./scripts/trust-task-coverage.sh` — 28 suites green, **0 violations**, coverage **48/109**
- `cargo fmt --all --check`

Refs #1059

title: fix(extension): accept both spellings of a re-cased error code (#126)
body:
fix(extension): accept both spellings of a re-cased error code (#126)

trust-tasks #279 re-cased ~200 extended error codes to the lowerCamelCase
SPEC §4.10 rule 4 requires: `provision/integration:context_required` became
`provision/integration:contextRequired`. Only the local part after the `:`
moved; namespaces are unchanged, and retired specs were deliberately left
snake_case.

`onboard-view.tsx` gated the onboarding context picker on a `===` against the
old spelling. Against a VTA that has taken #279 that comparison goes false and
nothing else happens: no error, no crash, no log — the picker just stops
appearing, and an operator with a multi-context VTA is dead-ended at Connect
with a message about a context they were never offered a way to choose.

Swapping the literal would move the defect rather than fix it. This wallet is
on the matching side of the wire, never the declaring side, and it updates on
the Chrome Web Store's schedule while the VTA updates on its own. A wallet
installed today still talks to a months-old agent next year; a wallet that has
not auto-updated meets an agent that took #279 this morning. Either literal is
correct for exactly half the deployed fleet, so both spellings have to match.

`matchesTrustTaskCode(actual, canonical)` (`trust-tasks/error-code.ts`) takes
the canonical camelCase code and accepts either spelling, deriving the
snake_case form rather than carrying a hand-maintained pair. Call sites read as
the code the registry declares today and the compatibility lives in one place,
so retiring the fold is one edit rather than a sweep — its TODO names the
condition: a declared minimum vta-service floor at or above the release
carrying the re-cased codes, the way #125 made 0.18.0 a floor for the
dispatcher path. It is deliberately not a fuzzy compare; codes differing by
more than the §4.10 re-casing stay distinct, so a rename cannot become a
collision.

`PROVISION_CONTEXT_REQUIRED` is exported from `provision/send.ts` in the
registry's current spelling, following the `MEDIATOR_REQUIRED` precedent in
`bridge-protocol.ts`. The code crosses two message-passing hops (offscreen →
background → popup) and is forwarded verbatim at each: normalising in transit
would make the hops need redeploying in lockstep with the agent, and would hide
from the popup which side of the rename its peer is on.

The other three codes this repo names — `vault/delete:versionConflict`,
`vault/sign-trust-task:notSignable`, `vault/upsert:sealedSecretInvalid` — all
verified against the registry, and all appear only in doc comments. Those are
re-spelled to the current declaration with a note pointing at the matcher, so
the next site that starts branching on one starts from the right shape.

Left alone deliberately: `auth:consent_required` is a `details.reason` token,
not an extended error code (the registry declares no bare `auth:` namespace),
`e.p.msg.context_required` is a DIDComm problem-report code from a different
scheme, and `push/register:*` is still snake_case in the registry.

Seven new tests pin the dual-accept property itself, since that is what makes
the deploy order safe and a comment cannot hold it: an equality that goes false
raises nothing.

Lint (`tsc -b`) clean across all workspaces; build clean; 546 tests passing,
0 failing (was 539). Both CI bundle guards re-run by hand and pass.

**Ship this before the vta-service PR that emits the new spelling** (R3.7).

title: feat(didcomm,didcomm-v1,tsp): absorb a mediator redelivery instead of executing the task twice
body:
`trust-tasks-rs` 0.12.0 (#274) implemented the SPEC §7.2 item 11 duplicate-execution record and the freshness bound it needs, and wired both into `consume_inbound`. The bindings did not have them wired, so no DIDComm or TSP deployment enforced item 11 — while the crate CHANGELOGs already advertised the defence. This wires it, **on by default**, in the three bindings where it matters most, and fixes the producer side in the capability client. ## The scenario A mediator holds a queued message, forwards it, and the acknowledgement is lost. It forwards again. That is not an attack. `bindings/didcomm/0.2` §6 says a mediator "can drop, delay, reorder, and **re-deliver**"; `bindings/didcomm-v1/0.2` §6 records v1's freshness guarantee as "**None**"; `bindings/tsp/0.1` §7 says TSP data messages "do not inherently prevent replay", and §5.2's routed and nested carriage puts intermediaries on the path who may re-forward the sealed inner message. In all three, an ordinary transport retry with nobody hostile involved applies the `acl/grant` twice, releases the vault secret twice, moves the value twice. SPEC §10.1 is explicit that at the document layer a redelivery and a hostile replay are indistinguishable — which is exactly why §7.2 item 11 makes absorbing them a normative requirement rather than an anti-abuse measure. ## The record is keyed on the document `id`, not the transport identifier This is the correctness rule the whole change rests on, and it is easiest to see in the mediator case. **A redelivery is a *new* transport message carrying the *same* document.** On DIDComm v2.1 it arrives with a fresh `@id` (and, where the document set no `threadId`, potentially a fresh `thid`). On DIDComm v1 it arrives with a fresh `@id` too — `MessageV1::new` mints a UUID per message, and `MessageV1`'s own documentation says so: "this is the *transport* identifier … a Trust Task document's `id` is a different value with a different lifetime". On TSP nothing about the envelope repeats at all: sealing the same document again derives fresh ephemeral material, so the two envelopes share no bytes. So a record keyed on `@id` / `thid` / the TSP envelope would see two distinct messages, admit the second, and execute the task a second time — the precise failure item 11 exists to prevent. SPEC §7.2 (*Keying and comparison for item 11*) forbids the substitution in terms: "transport request identifiers, transport message identifiers, and execution handles **MUST NOT** substitute". The wiring keys on the document `id` structurally rather than by convention: each binding hands `consume_inbound` the parsed `TrustTask

`, and `consume_inbound` claims `doc.id`. The transport identifier is never in a position to substitute, because it is never passed. Each crate has a test that pins it, and each one **asserts the transport identifier differs before feeding both arrivals through**: | Crate | Test | What it asserts first | |---|---|---| | `-didcomm` | `redelivery_under_a_fresh_transport_id_is_absorbed` | unpacks both JWEs and asserts `message.id` differs | | `-didcomm-v1` | `redelivery_under_a_fresh_transport_id_is_absorbed` | asserts the two messages' `@id`s differ | | `-tsp` | `redelivery_under_a_fresh_transport_envelope_is_absorbed` | asserts the two sealed envelopes differ byte for byte | Each then asserts the handler ran **once**. ## What the bindings now do Each crate gains a consumer type — `DidcommConsumer`, `DidcommV1Consumer`, `TspConsumer` — holding the replay record and the freshness policy, with `receive` (unpack + guarded pipeline) and `consume` (guarded pipeline over a document the caller opened, e.g. from a mediator SDK's own delivery loop). None of the three previously ran an inbound pipeline of any kind: they stopped at `unpack_trust_task` and left assembly to the caller. They now route through `consume_inbound`, which already carries the seam — so the verdict handling is the framework's, identical across all three, and cannot drift per binding: | Verdict | Disposition (SPEC §7.2, *Disposition of a duplicate*) | |---|---| | `Fresh` | dispatch, then `record_response` | | `Duplicate { prior_response: Some(r), .. }` | return `r`; **do not** re-dispatch | | `Duplicate { in_flight: true, .. }` | report the running execution rather than begin another | | `Duplicate { prior_response: None, in_flight: false }` | silence — fire-and-forget has no response to return | | `Conflict` | `idConflict` | | `Err(ReplayGuardError)` | **fail closed**: `unavailable`, `retryable = true`, no dispatch, and the store's identity stays out of the wire message (§10.4) | A claim held by an execution that then fails retryably is released, so a legitimate §8.4 retry is not blocked forever. `FreshnessPolicy` is wired on the same path and defaults to `consequential()` (`issuedAt` REQUIRED, five-minute window). Its `record_expiry` is what supplies `retain_until` to `claim` — SPEC §7.2 makes the acceptance window and the record's retention **one bound**, so `with_freshness` widens both together. There is no second TTL. ## Defaults, and the opt-out Consistent with the fail-closed defaults of #271 and #272, the record is **on** by default, backed by an in-process `InMemoryReplayGuard`. `with_replay_guard(Arc)` takes a store shared across replicas — the in-process guard is wrong behind a load balancer, and its rustdoc says so. `without_replay_record()` is the explicit opt-out, whose rustdoc states what it re-opens; a test (`the_opt_out_re_opens_double_execution`) demonstrates the redelivery executing twice under it, which is also the pre-change behaviour of these crates. ## The producer side: `trust-tasks-capability-client` Audited. The builders were already correct — `build_document`, and every family builder over it, mints a fresh `urn:uuid:` `id` and stamps `issuedAt` on **every** call, so rebuilding a request has always been a new attempt rather than a reuse. The gap was the *other* intent: re-sending a document already built and possibly signed. The crate offered nothing for it, which left a caller to re-stamp `issuedAt` and re-sign under the old `id` — exactly the document a 0.12 consumer now rejects with `idConflict`, since the digest covers `proof`. `new_attempt(&previous)` closes that: same addressing, type and payload under a fresh `id` and a fresh `issuedAt`, with `proof` dropped because it committed to the old `id`. Its rustdoc states the correlation consequence — where the previous request opened its own exchange, §4.9 names that exchange by the document `id`, so a new attempt opens a new one and the caller must hold the new `correlation_thread`; an explicit `threadId` is preserved. A test drives all three cases (identical resend → absorbed, reused `id` with altered content → `Conflict`, `new_attempt` → `Fresh`) through the real `InMemoryReplayGuard` rather than restating the rule in prose. ## Specs `bindings/didcomm/0.2` §6, `didcomm-v1/0.2` §6 and `tsp/0.1` §7 said replay defence was the consumer's job and named no mechanism. Each now carries a subsection that names it (§6.1, §6.1, §7.1): keyed on the document `id` with the transport identifiers explicitly excluded, comparison over the whole document, retention and acceptance window as one bound, the disposition of a duplicate, the fail-closed rule, and the shared-store requirement for a replicated consumer. All three are `status: draft`, so per SPEC §5.2 they are amended in place; no existing rule is weakened and no required member removed. `npm run validate` passes. ## Versions Defaulting the record on changes what a consumer observes — an undated document, and a second copy of one already executed, are now refused — so each binding is a leading-component bump: `-didcomm` 0.12.0 → **0.13.0**, `-didcomm-v1` 0.11.0 → **0.12.0**, `-tsp` 0.11.0 → **0.12.0**. `-capability-client` 0.11.0 → **0.12.0**: its API addition is additive, but a producer built against 0.11 will start meeting `idConflict` from consumers it previously reached and `issuedAt` is now required by the bindings' defaults, so it moves with them. Each `trust-tasks-rs` requirement stays at `"0.12"` — no cascade. No Rust or TS bindings were regenerated. ## Verification ``` cargo build --workspace Finished cargo test --workspace 38 suites ok, 0 failed cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -D warnings Finished cargo fmt --all --check clean RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --no-deps --all-features Generated npm run validate 349 specs, pre-existing warnings only ``` 21 new tests (7 per binding) plus 4 in the capability client. ## Scope Touches `trust-tasks-didcomm/`, `trust-tasks-didcomm-v1/`, `trust-tasks-tsp/`, `trust-tasks-capability-client/` and their three binding specs only. `trust-tasks-https/`, `bindings/https/0.2/` and `trust-tasks-rs/` are deliberately untouched — the HTTPS server runs its own pipeline and is being wired separately.

title: feat(https): keep the SPEC §7.2 item 11 duplicate-execution record, on by default
body:
## What an HTTPS deployment could do before this PR, and cannot now

`trust-tasks-rs` 0.12.0 (#274) implemented SPEC §7.2 item 11's duplicate-execution record and the §7.2 item 13 freshness bound, and wired both into `consume_inbound`. **The HTTPS server never calls `consume_inbound`** — it runs its own §7.2 pipeline in `src/server.rs`. So neither applied to it, while the crate's CHANGELOG advertised that the defence existed.

Concretely, against `main`:

* **The same document executed as many times as it arrived.** A `POST` of a captured `acl/grant` body — or an ordinary client, proxy or load-balancer retry of one — granted the ACL entry again, every time. §8.4 tells producers that retrying is safe *precisely because* item 11 obliges the consumer to absorb the resend; over this binding nobody was absorbing it.
* **A *different* document under a reused `id` was executed rather than refused.** Item 11 requires `idConflict` and forbids treating it as a retry of the original.
* **A document stamped a year ago, or a year hence, was accepted.** `validate_basic` honours `expiresAt`, which is optional; `issuedAt` was parsed and never looked at. A captured body stayed executable indefinitely.
* **The deserializer's rendering reached the wire.** Both places the server deserialized a body did `format!("{e}")` on a `serde_json::Error`, producing e.g. `payload does not match https://trusttasks.org/spec/acl/list/0.1: invalid type: string "not-a-number", expected a nonzero u64` — the member path, the expected type, and on the other path the byte offset. That is the §10.4 leak #274 closed everywhere else; it exported `RejectReason::malformed_from_serde` for exactly this and left it unused.

`bindings/https/0.2/spec.md` §5 said "Freshness / replay: **None**" and delegated both to the consumer without ever saying what the consumer had to do.

None of that is true after this PR.

## Where the claim sits in the pipeline, and why

Immediately before dispatch — after `Content-Type`, body parse, bearer auth, route lookup, `resolve_parties`, `validate_basic`, the freshness bound, the attribution gate, the DID-method pre-screen and proof verification.

That point is the `validated → accepted` transition of Framework 0.5.0's lifecycle table (spec repo PR #2): the last instant at which the server can still refuse a document for a reason that has nothing to do with having seen it before, and the first at which it has committed to execute.

* **Claiming earlier** would write a record for documents the server then refuses. Every malformed, stale, unattributable or badly-signed arrival would burn its `id`, a corrected resend would come back `idConflict` for the whole retention window, and a stranger could pre-burn an `id` it had merely observed.
* **Claiming later** is not a claim: the effect would already have happened.

One check runs after the claim — the per-spec policy (`enforce_spec_policy`) inside the dispatch closure, which needs the typed payload only that closure can produce. A refusal there releases the claim, so nothing is burned by it either. A panicking handler releases it too, then re-raises the panic unchanged: an `id` burned until `retain_until`, with every honest resend absorbed in silence, is worse than re-running an effect whose completion nobody can establish anyway.

## Disposition of every verdict

| Verdict | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `Fresh` | dispatch, then `record_response` | so the next arrival is answered with the result rather than re-executed |
| `Duplicate { prior_response: Some(r) }` | `200` with `r`, **no second dispatch** | §7.2: "the consumer SHOULD return the previously determined result" |
| `Duplicate { in_flight: true }` | `202 Accepted`, empty body | see below |
| `Duplicate { prior_response: None, in_flight: false }` | `204 No Content` | §7.2: "where the specification defines no success response, silence is the correct disposition" |
| `Conflict` | `409` `idConflict` | §7.2 item 11 |
| `Err(ReplayGuardError)` | `503` `unavailable`, `retryable = true`, **never executes** | a consumer that cannot establish whether a document is a duplicate has not satisfied item 11 |
| an unrecognised verdict (`ReplayVerdict` is `#[non_exhaustive]`) | the same `unavailable` path | a verdict this binding does not understand is not a licence to execute |

No path reports a duplicate as `taskFailed`. §7.2 is explicit: "the task did not fail, it already happened."

The guard error's detail — which in the test fixture names a Redis host — stays in the operator's log; `From<ReplayGuardError> for RejectReason` discards it rather than putting it on the wire.

### The in-flight-duplicate decision: `202 Accepted`, empty body

SPEC says the consumer "**SHOULD** return or expose the existing execution state rather than begin another". HTTP has one status that means *accepted, outcome not yet available*, and it is `202`.

The alternatives are each a lie about something:

* **`200`** would claim a result exists. It does not — the first delivery is still executing.
* **`409 Conflict`** would report a conflict. There is none; this is the *same* document, which is the case item 11 exists to absorb.
* **any `4xx`/`5xx` error document** would report a failure. Nothing failed, and §7.2 rules that reading out explicitly.
* **blocking until the first execution finishes and returning its result** would be the most helpful answer, and is what a future revision could do. It is not what this PR does: it would hold a connection for the duration of an execution the caller did not start, turn a duplicate delivery into an amplification primitive against the request-timeout and concurrency budgets, and it needs a wait-for-completion seam the `ReplayGuard` trait does not have.

`202` with an empty body is the honest, non-committal answer: *accepted, being executed, ask again*. `ClientError::DuplicateAbsorbed` surfaces it (and the `204`) to a typed caller as its own variant rather than as a response-decode failure, with rustdoc stating plainly that it is not a failure.

## Freshness

`FreshnessPolicy::consequential()` is the default — `issuedAt` REQUIRED, five-minute acceptance window — configurable via `.freshness(..)`. Its `record_expiry` is what supplies `retain_until` to `claim`: SPEC §7.2 (*Bounding the record*) makes the acceptance window and the record's retention **the same bound**, so there is deliberately no second TTL. A document the policy cannot place in any window is refused rather than executed on, per §7.2's "**MUST NOT** execute a *consequential Trust Task* on it".

## Binding spec

`bindings/https/0.2/spec.md` is `status: draft` (confirmed in its front matter), so per SPEC §5.2 it is amended in place. No existing rule is weakened.

* §4 gains rows for `202`, `204` and `409 idConflict` — the last was already this crate's behaviour and had no row.
* §5's security-profile row no longer says "Freshness / replay: **None**". It now says there is none *at the transport layer* — the captured body still arrives, and nothing in HTTP stops it — and points at the new §5.1.
* **§5.1 *Freshness and duplicate execution*** names the consumer obligation §5 previously left to inference: key on the document `id` alone (no `Idempotency-Key` substitute), reject a different document under a reused `id`, claim at the commit-to-execute point, answer duplicates per §4, fail closed when the record cannot be consulted, share the record across replicas, and retain it for the same bound as the acceptance window.

## Tests

Nine new tests in `trust-tasks-https/tests/end_to_end.rs`. Each was run against the pre-change server (`src/` reverted, the five tests that call the new builder methods stripped so the rest would compile) and **all seven that can compile there fail**:

```
failures:
    a_future_dated_document_is_refused_and_never_dispatched
    a_stale_document_is_refused_and_never_dispatched
    different_document_under_a_reused_id_is_an_id_conflict
    document_parse_failure_does_not_leak_the_serde_path
    duplicate_is_answered_with_the_recorded_response
    identical_resend_does_not_dispatch_the_handler_twice
    payload_deserialisation_failure_does_not_leak_the_serde_path
```

The suite:

* `identical_resend_does_not_dispatch_the_handler_twice` — asserts on the **handler's** invocation count, not the response: a server that answered identically while executing twice would pass a response-only test and still be the bug.
* `duplicate_is_answered_with_the_recorded_response` — byte-identical to the first answer, and a `#response` document rather than a `trust-task-error`.
* `different_document_under_a_reused_id_is_an_id_conflict` — `409`, and the conflicting document is never dispatched.
* `guard_error_fails_closed_to_unavailable_and_does_not_dispatch` — `503`, `retryable: true`, zero dispatches, and the guard's Redis host is absent from the wire message.
* `duplicate_with_no_recorded_response_is_silence_not_a_failure` — `204`, empty body.
* `in_flight_duplicate_is_accepted_not_re_executed` — `202`, empty body, zero dispatches. Driven by a guard that reports the verdict rather than by racing two live deliveries: whether a second request overlaps the first is a property of the runtime's scheduling, while the *disposition* of an in-flight duplicate is a property of this binding.
* `a_refused_dispatch_releases_the_claim` — a refusal is re-evaluated on resend, not absorbed as a duplicate of a rejection.
* `replay_protection_false_restores_the_undefended_path` — the opt-out does exactly what its rustdoc warns.
* `a_stale_document_is_refused_and_never_dispatched`, `a_future_dated_document_is_refused_and_never_dispatched`, `a_widened_window_accepts_what_the_default_refuses` — the freshness bound and its one knob.
* `payload_deserialisation_failure_does_not_leak_the_serde_path`, `document_parse_failure_does_not_leak_the_serde_path` — no member name, no offset, no expected-type on the wire.

One existing fixture was corrected rather than left silently weakened: `https_enforces_recipient_required_with_no_in_band_recipient` carried no `issuedAt`, so under the new default it would have been refused at the freshness check with the *same* `malformedRequest`/400 — passing while never reaching the recipient-REQUIRED check it exists to exercise. It now carries `issuedAt`, with a comment saying why.

## Verification

Actual output, run from the worktree with `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` set inside it:

```
$ cargo build --workspace --all-features
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.73s

$ cargo test --workspace --all-features
35 × "test result: ok"; 0 failed. trust-tasks-https: 45 passed (integration), 10 passed (unit), 4 doc-tests ignored.

$ cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.71s

$ cargo fmt --all --check
(exit 0, no output)

$ RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --no-deps --all-features
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 1.40s
   Generated .../target/doc/trust_tasks_capability_client/index.html and 8 other files

$ npm run validate
Validated 349 specs, indexed 65 shared schemas.
(only the pre-existing warnings on main)
```

## Versioning

`trust-tasks-https` 0.12.0 → **0.13.0**, with a CHANGELOG entry. **This is breaking**, said plainly: defaulting the guard *and* the freshness bound ON changes what a consumer observes. A deployment that resends under a reused `id` now sees `idConflict`; one whose producers omit `issuedAt`, or whose intermediaries hold a request longer than five minutes, now sees `malformedRequest` / `expired` where the document used to be executed. `ClientError` also gains a variant. The safe behaviour is the default, as with `require_attribution` in 0.11.0; both opt-outs are one builder call and both say what they cost.

The `trust-tasks-rs` requirement stays at `"0.12"` — `ReplayGuard` ships in 0.12.0, so there is no cascade. `Cargo.lock` moves by exactly one line.

No Rust or TS bindings were regenerated.
